# Optimisation: Get more out of the AI you’re already using.

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/services/optimalisatie

> AITJE to improve your AI workflow, chatbot or agent. Optimise skills, rules, reusable code, tool calls, knowledge bases, RAG and models in a targeted manner.

Whether it’s a workflow, chatbot, internal knowledge search tool, voice agent or coding agent: if you’re already using AI, there’s often more to be gained. AITJE investigates where time, context and computational power are being wasted, and where results can be improved.

This may be found in an agent’s instructions and skills, the structure of your knowledge base, the tool calls or the model itself. AITJE draws up an improvement plan and can implement the chosen changes. This applies even if you or another party has built the solution, either in-house or via external services.

## Who it is for

- A workflow involving many calls or repetitive tasks
- A chatbot that lacks the right knowledge
- A voice or coding agent that needs to work better
- High costs or inconsistent results

## The approach

### Measuring and analysing

AITJE It tracks your current tasks: what context is provided to the model, what does the knowledge base find, and where do errors, extra calls or delays occur?

### Improvement plan

Targeted adjustments to instructions, code, knowledge, retrieval or models. Including priorities, expected impact and the required hours and costs.

### Select & customise

You choose which improvements are to be implemented. Once the scope and hours have been agreed, AITJE will implement the agreed changes.

### Retest

The same sample tasks are carried out again. Quality, speed, calls and costs are compared with the initial situation.

## Deliverables

- An overview of your current operations and consumption
- An improvement plan for context, knowledge, code and models
- Priorities with expected impact, hours and costs
- After implementation: a comparison based on the agreed test tasks

## Prices and conditions

Fixed hourly rate. All prices exclude VAT.

For research and the improvement plan. Changes to the workflow, knowledge base or models are quoted separately, either by the hour or as a project. You give your approval in advance for the work to be carried out.

### Guardrailcheck

Approximately four hours for a single defined workflow: checking boundaries, human oversight, error handling and logging, and conducting targeted testing. You will receive the findings; any adjustments will be quoted separately.

From €299. All prices exclude VAT.

## Agreed separately

- Implementation of improvements (separate, at your discretion)
- External licences, API costs, hardware and server capacity
- A guarantee of a precise technical or financial result

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AITJE improve my existing AI?

Yes. ‘AITJE’ examines how your current workflow, chatbot, knowledge search tool, voice agent or coding agent works. The improvement plan may cover instructions, skills, code, tool calling, the knowledge base, RAG or model selection. You choose which adjustments ‘AITJE’ carries out.

### Even if another party has built the solution?

Yes, provided AITJE is given sufficient information and access to carry out the work responsibly.

### How do skills, rules and documentation help an agent?

They make the working method explicit: which steps an agent must follow, which code and tools already exist, and how the codebase is structured. ‘AITJE’ can organise instructions, Markdown files, skills and the folder structure more effectively. Reusable code and targeted tool calls prevent the model from having to figure everything out or generate it from scratch for every task.

### Can AITJE reorganise my knowledge base and vector database?

Yes. ‘AITJE’ can restructure documents and categories and improve the organisation of text sections, dates, priorities and access rights. The embedding model, index and search method can also be customised. If a different embedding model is used, the relevant documents are reprocessed and re-indexed. It is then tested whether RAG retrieves knowledge that is more relevant to your queries.

### What if the knowledge base and the questions use different languages?

AITJE It checks whether the embedding model adequately supports the languages used and whether the search query could be better formulated or translated. A multilingual embedding model or a different search approach may help. The choice is tested using your queries and documents, ensuring that the meaning and the correct source are retained.

### Does ‘AITJE’ also use the terms ‘fine-tuning’ and ‘ablation’?

Where appropriate for the task and the model. Fine-tuning uses examples to further train the task behaviour. Ablation alters a model’s rejection behaviour using available weights; this may be relevant when legitimate requests are unnecessarily rejected. It does not add any up-to-date business knowledge. ‘AITJE’ compares a modified version with the original version against the agreed tasks and checks.

### How do I know if an optimisation really makes a difference?

The same types of tasks are assessed both before and after the adjustment. AITJE looks at the usability of the result, speed, number of calls, resource usage and correction work. Fewer tokens or a cheaper model is only useful if the solution continues to meet the agreed quality standards.

### Is a Guardrailcheck a certification?

No. It is a practical technical assessment, not a legal judgement or a guarantee that a system will never make mistakes.

# Safe use of AI: Greater control over your AI and your data.

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/services/veilig-ai-gebruik

> AITJE Helps limit AI usage through anonymisation, role-based access rights for RAG, guardrails, human oversight and budget limits. Insight into data locations and retention policies.

Safe AI usage begins before you send anything to a model. What information is really necessary? Is this employee authorised to use that data? Can names, contact details and other identifiable details be removed? AITJE helps you incorporate these choices into your workflow.

This is followed by checks on responses, actions and costs. With appropriate guardrails, staff approval, logging and limits, you determine what the solution is permitted to do. ‘AITJE’ also examines where data is processed and stored, and when processing within your own environment is more appropriate.

## Who it is for

- Teams that process customer data using AI
- Knowledge bases with different access rights
- Agents that carry out actions in your systems
- Organisations wishing to gain control over usage and costs

## The approach

### Taking stock

Which data goes to which model? Who has access, what actions are possible and how is usage restricted?

### Institutions & locations

AITJE It examines processing, storage, training settings, retention periods and existing controls. Unknown information remains identifiable.

### Selecting measures

A proposal for data minimisation, role-based access rights, guardrails, confirmation and limits. You choose which adjustments are necessary.

### Set-up & testing

Implementation is agreed separately. AITJE tests the chosen measures, including in the event of unauthorised access, unwanted instructions and exceeded limits.

## Deliverables

- Overview of data flows, providers and data locations
- Insight into access, retention policies and existing controls
- Points for consideration with practical suggestions for improvement
- Following agreed implementation: measures set up and tested

## Prices and conditions

From €225. All prices exclude VAT.

For a simple AI data location check, allow approximately three hours for a limited number of known services. The basic inventory is already included in the AI scan; we reuse previous findings. In-depth technical research and implementation are subject to a separate hourly estimate. The services to be examined and the scope of delivery are agreed in advance.

### AI-datalocatiecheck

A targeted review of a limited number of known AI services, available provider information and settings. Approximately three hours for a straightforward situation. We reuse findings from a scan; uncertainties remain visible.

From €225. All prices exclude VAT.

### Practical measures

Anonymisation, role-based access rights in RAG, guardrails, employee confirmation, budget limits and logging. The chosen adjustments will be agreed in advance.

Fixed hourly rate. All prices exclude VAT.

### AI-wegwijs

Explanations, guidelines and resources for working with AI smartly and securely, either as part of your collaboration or on its own.

- A binding legal opinion, certification or guarantee of compliance

- Extensive follow-up research

## Frequently asked questions

### How much does an AI data location check cost?

From €225 excluding VAT for a straightforward scenario, estimated at approximately three hours. We check a pre-agreed, limited number of known AI services, settings and available provider information. The basic assessment forms part of the AI scan. We reuse previous findings; additional technical research and measures are quoted separately.

### How does ‘AITJE’ help ensure the safe use of AI?

AITJE It maps out data flows, access, data locations and settings, and can implement practical measures. These include deleting personal data prior to an external model call, role-based access rights for the knowledge base, human verification, guardrails, usage limits and logging. The scope of the investigation and implementation is defined in advance.

### Can AITJE remove personal data before it is sent to an external model?

Yes. AITJE can incorporate a local preparatory step that removes or replaces names, contact details and other identifiable details, and forwards only the necessary information. Whether the result is truly anonymous also depends on the wider context. Replacing a name with a label does not automatically constitute full anonymisation.

### Would it help to start a new, blank chat each time?

A new context for each task or client limits which previous messages are passed on to the next query. AITJE can separate sessions, memory and context. This does not automatically change what the provider itself stores or uses for training: those settings and agreements are checked separately.

### Can usage for training or data storage be disabled?

AITJE checks which settings and options are available for the selected service. Disabling the use of data for training is not the same as not storing any data. Zero-data retention may be available for certain APIs and functions, subject to conditions and exceptions. AITJE will investigate what actually applies to your specific use case.

### How can you prevent an employee from accessing restricted documents via AI?

The application verifies the identity and role before RAG retrieves data. The search query is restricted to authorised documents, text passages and categories. The same permissions apply to tool calls and other integrations. Restricted content should therefore not first be provided to the model with only the instruction not to share it.

### Can AITJE protect against prompt injection and jailbreaks?

AITJE It can combine multiple checks: verifying input and retrieved documents, separating instructions from source material, restricting tool permissions and validating actions. A filter layer or LLM firewall can help with this, but does not stop every attack. That is why access and permitted actions are also enforced and tested outside the model.

### Can AI costs and the number of calls be limited?

Yes. AITJE can configure budgets, limits per task and user, rate limiting and a maximum number of attempts. Before a new call, the application can check whether there is still budget available. Provider warnings do not always result in an immediate halt; therefore, the system checks which limits actually cause a block. Ongoing calls and delayed usage reporting are taken into account in the configuration.

### When must an employee confirm an action?

This is agreed in advance. For example, before a message is sent, a payment is processed or important data is amended. The employee sees the proposal and the consequences and must give their explicit consent before the action is carried out. The confirmation and execution can be logged.

### How are responses and actions monitored?

AITJE It can link responses to authorised sources via RAG and check output against code for format, required fields and permitted actions. A second model, LLM-as-a-Judge, can provide additional oversight. RAG and a second model can help identify errors, but do not rule them out entirely. For important outcomes, human assessment remains an appropriate check.

### What is logged internally?

For example, who initiated a task, which sources and model versions were used, what action was proposed, who gave approval and what was carried out. AITJE determines the level of detail, access and retention period. Personal data, full prompts and API keys do not need to be included in a log file by default.

### Is running systems locally always sufficient to protect data?

Processing locally can prevent content from being sent to an external model provider. The environment itself still requires appropriate network security, access rights and management. AITJE also checks connections, logging and fallback routes to ensure that confidential data is not sent via an alternative route.

### Is a Dutch server automatically secure?

No. A location tells you something, but not everything. ‘AITJE’ also looks at who has access, what is being stored and which settings are enabled.

### Does this replace a lawyer or a data protection officer?

No. ‘AITJE’ handles the technical side: where data goes and what measures are possible. For a legal opinion, you’ll need a specialist.

## Contact

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# 350 clients. One central workspace.

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/cases/council-hub

> Following a takeover, a marketing company’s client base grew from 150 to 350. AITJE brought together client data, tickets, projects, invoicing information and call transcripts in a central hub. Staff can search for and chat with their business experts, with access based on their role and AI integrated into an existing Mac mini.

Case study — Marketing / customer management, tickets & business knowledge

The marketing company worked with 150 clients. Following a takeover, 200 clients were added to this. The client portfolio grew to 350, but the information was still scattered across various applications and teams.

When the phone rang, the employee didn’t immediately know what was going on. Was there an open ticket? Who was working on the project? Had anyone called back yet? And were there any outstanding invoices? Finding the answer always required searching through multiple systems.

AITJE It has built a central management hub where staff can quickly search by customer name, company name or website. The relevant data is brought together via API connections. In addition, they can ask questions via a RAG chat that utilises synchronised business knowledge.

## The approach

### Connect

Code connects the hub to external applications via API and MCP integrations. Toolcalling provides the language model with defined ways to query the connected platforms.

### Synchronise

Three times a day, the selected company data is retrieved and converted into vector embeddings. The local vector database makes this knowledge available to the RAG chat.

### Search & retrieve

A name, company or website links to the available customer context. For a chat enquiry, RAG retrieves relevant passages; tool calls can also consult data from linked applications where these are accessible.

### Responses with access

Qwen formulates the response using the available context. Access is restricted within the hub and when retrieving data based on the employee’s role, ensuring that the chat operates solely with authorised information.

# 25 New game levels every week. With no external token costs.

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/cases/coder-game-in-24-uur

> A marketing agency took over an existing mobile puzzle game but ran into difficulties when creating new levels. AITJE analysed the game, built a reusable level design system and linked AITJE Coder to Qwen on its own server. Now, the agency 25 creates new levels every week from a single assignment in OpenCode.

Case study — Marketing agency / level design & in-house coding agency

The marketing agency had acquired a mobile game from a development agency. It was a puzzle game in the style of Candy Crush: the app was fully functional and already live. The agency was able to market the game, but had less experience in managing and expanding the code.

New levels became the stumbling block. A marketer used AI to build them, but each task essentially started from scratch. There was no fixed system for the structure, reusable components or the level of difficulty. As a result, gaps kept appearing in the process.

## The approach

### Opening the correct repository

The marketer opens the game project in OpenCode using the ‘AITJE Coder’ approach. In this way, the agent works with the game’s existing code, components and level design system.

### A series of questions covering25-levels

The brief is now clear: create new levels for 25 based on the design system and the existing level registration. The rules and context are already set out in the project.

### Let Qwen carry on working

The agent uses a Qwen3 API endpoint (6-35B-A3B) on a server under its own management. The development loop generates the level sequence using the reusable components and the information on pace and difficulty.

### Building on the system

The agency is currently operating at a rate of 25 new levels per week. New projects use the same foundation, making scaling up a repeatable process.

# From technical drawing to 3D product model.

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/cases/3d-productmodellen-met-ai

> AITJE built a workflow for a partner specialising in contact cables that converts product data and technical drawings from WordPress into 3D models. AITJE Coder controls Blender; Three.js makes the GLB files usable on the website. Following optimisation, API costs fell from approximately €9 to €0.11–€0.18 per product.

Case study — Power leads / 3D catalogue & workflow optimisation

With connector cables, the details make all the difference: the shape of a connector, the position of the contacts and the way a cable connects. A photograph shows just one side. A rotatable 3D model helps customers view the product from multiple angles.

Our partner has a catalogue of more than 10,000 products. Manually creating a model and a series of images for each product was prohibitively expensive on that scale. AITJE therefore built a repeatable workflow based on the product data and technical drawings that were already in the WordPress CMS.

## The approach

### Collect product

A targeted tool call retrieves the product, the associated data and the technical drawing from WordPress. The agent receives the information for this task without having to search through the entire website themselves.

### Loading instructions

A fixed prompt and structured Markdown instructions describe the modelling rules, materials, output and checks. The agent does not need to reinvent the workflow for every product.

### Controlling Blender

AITJE Coder Uses OpenCode in automatic mode, connected to GPT-6Astra via the OpenAIAPI. Using Blender MCP, the agent builds the geometry based on the retrieved drawing and product information.

### Export to GLB

The model is exported as a GLB: a file in which geometry and materials are stored together. The CMS links the output to the correct product, so that the result is included in the catalogue.

### Display on the website

Three.js loads the GLB model into the browser. Customers can rotate the product and view it from multiple angles. GSAP handles the presentation and movement within the interface.

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# Your firm’s expertise. An assistant that works with it.

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/cases/documenten-doorzoeken-en-lakken

> For an estate agency, AITJE linked Realworks, email inboxes and Google Drive to its own AI assistant. Staff chat with the knowledge relevant to their role. The website chatbot uses a separate, carefully selected knowledge base from the same environment.

Case study — Estate agency / In-house expertise & website chat

At an estate agency, information is rarely stored in one place. Property details are in Realworks, appointments and correspondence are in the email inbox, and documents are in Google Drive. Finding an answer often means switching between systems and deciding for yourself which information is still up to date.

AITJE installed the Assistant on a Linux server, linked to an BOSGAME M5. The existing sources are consolidated into a dedicated knowledge base. Staff ask their questions in a single chat; the search layer retrieves relevant information, with the correct date, category and access rights.

## The approach

### Synchronise

The knowledge from the linked sources is synchronised three times a day. This ensures that new and amended data is incorporated into the knowledge base.

### Organising & embedding

The content is divided into searchable text fragments. Harrier creates vector embeddings; category, date, source, priority and access rights remain linked to the knowledge.

### Targeted search

When a question is asked, RAG searches for relevant content within the knowledge that the employee is authorised to use. The date and priority help to select the correct information.

### Formulating a response

GPT-OSS-120B uses the passages it finds to construct the answer. Business knowledge is retrieved when needed; an entire file is not sent to the model every time.

## Contact

# 6,900 Products enriched and translated in 7 hours

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/cases/productteksten-zonder-tokenkosten

> AITJE built a workflow for a leading Dutch online shop specialising in chargers that supplements product descriptions with technical charging data, translates them for four markets and uploads them directly back into the CMS. Without any external costs per AI token.

Case study — E-commerce / Chargers & electronics

## The approach

### Product data

Via the CMS integration, the workflow retrieves the current products, descriptions and available specifications. This means the analysis begins with the catalogue that the online shop is already using.

### Charging data

Gemma can use toolcalls to retrieve specific information from charging databases. Benchmarks for each charger and device supplement the existing product data.

### Enrich

Gemma 4 31B analyses the original text and the retrieved data. Code processes the load data and calculations; the model then converts this into comprehensible product information.

### Translate

A Gemma-based translation step adapts the enriched information for the German, Belgian, Luxembourgish and French markets. Specifications and product information remain part of the translation workflow.

### Publish

The workflow writes the new texts and translations back to the corresponding products via the CMS integration. This publication was already included during the initial processing: the content did not need to be transferred manually afterwards.

# What is generative AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-generatieve-ai

> Generative AI creates new content based on a prompt: text, images, music, video, 3D or code. What happens during the generation process, and how do you turn an interesting result into something useful for your work?

### In brief

Generative AI is the collective term for models capable of creating new content. For example, you provide a question, description, image or sound clip, and the model generates an output. This could be a draft text, but also an illustration, a spoken explanation or a piece of software. ‘Generative’ refers to the creation of output; it does not mean that this output is automatically correct, original or suitable for publication.

### How can a model create something new?

During training, a model learns patterns from examples. This knowledge is captured in model parameters. During use – also known as inference – a query is processed using those learnt patterns. A language model typically constructs a sequence of tokens; an image model can generate an image through successive steps. You therefore do not usually retrieve a stored answer. The model calculates a new output within the limits of its training and the context provided.

### Generating is different from recognising

A system that recognises a document as an invoice is performing a classification task. A system that writes an accompanying email for that invoice is generating text. These tasks can occur within the same workflow. A model can also interpret images as well as write text. It helps to specify exactly what you need: recognition, lookup, calculation or creating something new. Not every step requires a generative model.

### A practical example

A team wants to make internal work instructions more accessible. The software first retrieves the current instruction. A language model then creates a brief explanation for a new employee. Another model may, if necessary, create a supporting image or spoken version. The original instruction remains the starting point. An employee checks the explanation before it is distributed. In this way, the system supports the generation of existing knowledge without taking over responsibility for the content.

### What determines a useful result?

The brief, available information, choice of model and desired output format all work together. A compelling example says little about all other briefs. Therefore, also test for missing information, differing phrasing and complex cases. For text, accuracy of content is key; for images, composition, for example; and for code, functionality is also important. A usable result meets the agreed requirements and fits within the process in which it is assessed or used.

### Where do you start as an organisation?

Choose one recurring task and describe what input is available, what the outcome should be and who checks it. Compare the time and cost of the entire task, including post-processing. Then determine whether local processing, an external API or a combination is suitable. Generative AI is particularly useful when the new content fits in with your day-to-day work at the right time and in the right form.

## Sources

- [IBM — Generative AI](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/generative-ai)
- [Hugging Face — Text generation with LLMs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/llm_tutorial)
- [Hugging Face — Components of a diffusion pipeline](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/quicktour)

# What is text generation using AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-tekstgeneratie

> Text generation is the process of creating text using a language model. From draft emails and summaries to structured responses: the task and the available information determine the output.

### In brief

In text generation, a language model generates text based on input. This may be new text or a reworking of existing information: shorter, clearer, in a different language or in an agreed structure. The result is a proposal generated by the model. It is not an automatic confirmation that names, figures, events and conclusions are correct. The level of verification required depends on the intended use.

### How does a language model construct text?

The input is converted into tokens: small chunks of text. The model calculates which subsequent tokens fit the prompt and the preceding context. This creates a response step by step. Settings can influence the selection and maximum length. This helps to guide the output, but changing a setting does not automatically make the model better informed. Missing facts must be derived from reliable data, not from a more creative answer.

### What information should you include?

A good brief describes the objective, target audience, tone and desired format. For company information, the correct sources are also required. Think of a product list, procedure or relevant passage from a document. A search step can be used to retrieve that information in a targeted manner. It is often unnecessary to send a complete archive. Select only what the task requires and make it clear which information the model must not fill in if it is missing.

### A practical example

An employee wants a draft reply to a customer enquiry. The software retrieves the relevant order and delivery details. The model receives only that data and drafts a short email in the desired tone. An employee checks the draft and sends it. Fixed details, such as the order number and amount, can be retrieved directly from the system. This means the language model does not need to invent facts that are already recorded in the accounts.

### From ad-hoc text to a fixed workflow

Text generation may form part of a larger application. For example, you could use separate steps for summarising, classifying and drafting a response. Structured output simplifies further processing, but the software still needs to check that structure. Missing fields, invalid values and extra text may occur. You should therefore clearly distinguish between a generated draft and a final, approved document.

### How do you assess quality and costs?

Test with real-world types of questions and check facts, completeness, tone and corrections. Also take into account the length of input and output: a lot of context or multiple attempts can result in additional computational work and API costs. A smaller model with targeted information may be sufficient for a well-defined task. The aim is to produce a usable text at a reasonable cost, not the longest answer or the largest number of tokens.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Text generation with LLMs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/llm_tutorial)
- [IBM — Generative AI](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/generative-ai)

# What is image generation?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-image-generation

> Image generation, or ‘beeldgeneratie’, enables AI to create new images or modify existing ones. A description or reference provides guidance; the model constructs the visual output.

### In brief

Image generation means that an AI model creates an image. The input can be a text description, a reference image or a combination of both. You can have a new image generated, explore variations or modify part of an existing image. The result is a visual interpretation of the prompt. The model therefore does not provide any evidence that a person, event, location or product depicted actually exists.

### What types of image generation are there?

In text-to-image, text forms the starting point. In image-to-image, an existing image guides the new output. Inpainting focuses on a selected area, whilst image expansion can create extra space around the original composition. Which functions are available depends on the model and the software. Some applications combine multiple models or processing steps rather than performing everything in a single command.

### What makes a description useful?

Describe the subject, setting, perspective, lighting and desired composition. Also indicate where space must be left for text or which details must be retained. A reference image can help with shape and proportions. A brief with many conflicting requirements makes verification more difficult. It is preferable to work with a clear basis and targeted adjustments. A seed can make variants comparable within the same environment, but is no guarantee of identical output on other systems.

### A practical example

An organisation is looking for an illustration for an internal presentation on maintenance. First, they determine which machine needs to be recognisable and which details are essential. The illustrator produces a few concepts, after which a member of staff selects and checks the best composition. For an image that needs to accurately depict a real product, photography or a controlled product render may be more suitable. The intended use determines which approach is both convincing and practical.

### Generating is not the same as understanding images

For example, a vision model interprets a photograph or a document image. A generative image model creates or edits an image. These functions can work together, but they are distinct tasks. A system can first analyse a photograph and then prepare an editing task. Understanding an image does not automatically mean that the system can also accurately reconstruct that image. Assess both steps separately when combining them in a workflow.

### From concept to usable visual

Check details, perspective, text within the image and consistency with other images. Select the required resolution based on the final format; a larger file does not automatically correct errors. Record the chosen settings and versions if you want a consistent image series. Also take into account the permitted use of the model and reference material. Generation, selection and post-processing together form the production process.

- [Hugging Face — Text-to-image](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/using-diffusers/conditional_image_generation)
- [Hugging Face — Components of a diffusion pipeline](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/quicktour)
- [Hugging Face — Reproducible generation](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/using-diffusers/reusing_seeds)

# What is music generation?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-music-generation

> Music generation is the process of creating music using AI based on, for example, style, atmosphere, instruments or a sound clip. The model generates a musical composition which you can then listen to and edit.

### In brief

Music generation means that an AI model creates new musical output. For example, you might describe a calm instrumental piece featuring a piano and a slow tempo. Depending on the model, existing audio can also serve as a guide. The result may be a short clip, an accompaniment or a more elaborate composition. A music model therefore does something different from compiling a playlist: it produces sound or a musical representation.

### How is music generated?

Models learn patterns in rhythm, sound and musical coherence. Some systems predict compact audio codes which are then converted into sound. Other generative techniques operate using successive processing steps. The method is not always the same as that used for text generation. The outputs also differ: one system produces an audio file, whilst another application may, for example, provide musical notes or individually editable components. Check exactly what output you are actually receiving.

### What should you include in a music commission?

Describe the purpose, the atmosphere, instrumentation, desired length and how prominent the music should be. Background music accompanying a spoken explanation requires a different approach to a recognisable opening. Words such as ‘calm’ or ‘energetic’ provide direction, but do not determine an exact composition. You should therefore listen to several versions and assess the clip in its final context. A standalone demo may sound pleasant but could still be too busy when played alongside a voice.

### A practical example

A team creates a short explanatory video and selects a subtle instrumental background track. They have various clips produced, choose a suitable version and edit it to accompany the spoken text. In doing so, they pay attention to volume, transitions and length. The generation is a single step; the final mix and editing remain important. For a fixed theme tune, greater control over the melody and arrangement may be required than a standard music commission offers.

### Where is the quality control?

Pay attention to abrupt transitions, repetition, unwanted sounds and the flow between the beginning and the end. For longer outputs, the musical coherence must also remain intact. Vocals, separate instrument tracks and precise tempo settings are not features that every model automatically supports. Assess what you need before choosing the workflow. A clip that sounds good straight away is not necessarily easy to edit further in your music software.

### What does this mean for a workflow?

Document how commissioning, selection, assembly and storage are carried out. Save the chosen variant with the settings used, so that a team knows which one it belongs to. Compare costs per usable clip rather than just per generation attempt. Also check which terms of use apply to the model and the input. A locally available model may be an option, but it requires sufficient computing power and does not automatically offer the same features as an external music service.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — MusicGen](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/musicgen)
- [IBM — Generative AI](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/generative-ai)

# What is speech and audio generation?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-spraak-en-audiogeneratie

> With AI, you can convert text to speech and generate other sounds. How do text-to-speech, sound effects and transcription differ, and where do they fit into a practical workflow?

### In brief

Audio generation is the creation of sound using a model. Speech generation is a specific form of this: for example, written text is converted into a spoken explanation. Other applications create sound effects or a soundscape. Music also falls under generative audio, but has its own requirements in terms of rhythm and composition. The chosen task determines which model and which output are suitable; a single audio model does not necessarily support all these possibilities.

### What is text-to-speech?

Text-to-speech, often abbreviated to TTS, converts text into spoken audio. A model or application may offer settings for language, voice, speed or speaking style. This varies from system to system. The text remains important: abbreviations, numbers and brand names may be pronounced differently than expected. A text that is easy to read on paper does not always sound natural when read out verbatim.

### What is the difference between this and transcription?

Speech recognition converts existing audio into text. Speech synthesis works the other way round. You can combine both: a spoken question is transcribed, a language model prepares a response, and a TTS model reads that response aloud. These are separate steps, each with its own potential for error. For example, an incorrect transcription can result in an incorrect answer, even if the final voice sounds very natural.

### A practical example

An organisation wishes to provide a work instruction as a spoken explanation as well. First, the text is rewritten for listening: shorter sentences and clearly pronounced numbers. The audio is then recorded and listened to by someone familiar with the procedure. Only after verification is the file attached to the instruction. If the procedure changes, the spoken version must also be updated. This ensures that the text and audio always correspond to the same up-to-date information.

### What should you look out for when it comes to voice and sound?

Assess intelligibility, pronunciation, pauses and the volume of the output. Where multiple languages are involved, quality may vary from language to language. Furthermore, a selected voice is not the same as an imitation of a recognisable person’s voice. The use of such a voice requires clear agreements and the consent of the person concerned. For sound effects, the key consideration is whether the sound suits the event and remains sufficiently controllable during editing.

### How do you set up the processing?

Determine which text goes to the model, where audio files are stored and how regeneration works following a change. Also consider output length, waiting time and playback within your application. Costs may, for example, be related to character count, audio length or computational work, and do not necessarily have to follow the same token structure as a text API. A good workflow preserves the source content and makes it clear which version of the audio corresponds to it.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Text-to-speech](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tasks/text-to-speech)

- [IBM — Generative AI](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/generative-ai)

# What is AI-powered video generation?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-videogeneratie

> Video generation creates moving images from a description, an image or an existing clip. The model must not only produce attractive images, but also maintain continuity between successive frames.

### In brief

In video generation, an AI model calculates a sequence of images that together form movement. The prompt may be text or an image serving as a starting point. Some applications also edit existing video. A generated clip may be useful as a concept, supporting footage or part of a montage. It is not a recording of a real event, even when the result resembles a normal recording.

### From text or image to motion

With text-to-video, a description dictates the content. With image-to-video, a starting image already provides information about the subject and composition. The command can then direct the movement or camera. The level of control available varies by model. A described pan movement, exact number of actions or fixed duration is not always executed precisely. Use the capabilities of the chosen system as a starting point for your shot planning.

### Why is video more complicated than an image?

Consecutive frames must fit together seamlessly. A person, product or background must not change unintentionally as soon as something moves. Direction, speed and relative positions must also remain credible. Furthermore, the amount of information to be processed increases with length and resolution. A single, attractive still frame therefore says little about the video as a whole. Always assess the clip in motion and also look at the beginning, transitions and ending.

### A practical example

A team is producing an explanatory video about a new work process. The core of the video consists of real screen recordings of the application. An abstract moving image is generated for a short transition. The team selects a suitable clip and incorporates it into the edit. In this way, computer-generated imagery supports the narrative without replacing the software’s actual functionality with fictional screens. The choice between footage, animation and computer-generated imagery depends on what you want to show.

### What is involved in the production process?

Video generation does not automatically result in a fully edited film. Subtitles, voice-overs, sound, music and the editing of shots may be separate steps. Some models combine video and audio, whilst others do not. You should therefore specify which files you will receive and how they will be post-processed. Also check text, logos and product details where these are important. Where multiple shots are involved, ensuring recognisable continuity often requires additional selection and editing.

### How do you compare speed and costs?

Compare usable seconds of video, the number of attempts required and the post-production work. A short, low-resolution generation can serve primarily as a test, whilst the final format requires more processing power. Running locally requires suitable hardware; an external service can provide capacity with its own limits and rates. First, decide what level of quality and control is required. You can then determine whether generating content for this part of the process is truly a suitable production step.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Video generation](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/using-diffusers/text-img2vid)
- [Hugging Face — Components of a diffusion pipeline](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/quicktour)

# What is 3D generation using AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-3d-generatie

> 3D generation creates a digital spatial representation based on text or images. From concept object to textured model: the output is only usable when it is compatible with your design software and application.

### In brief

In 3D generation, AI creates a digital representation of a three-dimensional object or a scene. Text or one or more images can serve as input. Depending on the system, this results, for example, in a textured mesh or another spatial representation. This is different from a standard image that merely resembles a 3D object. A usable 3D file contains information that allows you to view the object from different angles or process it further.

### What are geometry and texture?

Geometry describes the shape of an object. A mesh uses points, edges and faces to represent this. A texture provides information about the appearance of surfaces, such as colour and detail. Material properties can also determine how light is rendered. A convincing texture can conceal a weak shape in a single view. You should therefore also examine the geometry and the back of the object, particularly when the model is being further modified.

### What can you deduce from an image?

A photograph shows only part of an object. A generative system must fill in the unseen sides based on learnt patterns. The result may be plausible without exactly matching the real object. Multiple useful views can provide more guidance, but do not rule out missing or incorrect details. For a product where dimensions and construction are important, verified design information remains essential.

### A practical example

A designer wishes to explore different shapes for a decorative object. AI generates a number of digital concepts viewed from various angles. The chosen shape is then refined and adapted in design software. For use in an interactive environment, for example, the size and level of detail are checked. This process accelerates the design phase, whilst the requirements of the final application determine how much post-processing is needed.

### 3D generation is not a ready-made CAD design

A generated object does not automatically have correct dimensions, an editable component structure or tolerances suitable for production. Nor does a visually appealing model automatically mean that it is suitable for printing. For 3D printing, the shape must, amongst other things, be usable as a closed volume and be suitable for the chosen production method. For games or web display, different requirements apply, such as file size and the number of faces. Each of these applications requires its own set of checks.

### How do you make output transferable?

Determine in advance which file type, scale and components the next step requires. Check whether geometry and textures are actually being exported and whether your software reads them correctly. Keep a record of the references and any adjustments made. Compare the entire process from concept to usable file, not just the first render. This will clarify whether AI generation saves time or mainly results in extra corrective work.

- [Tencent — Hunyuan3D 2.1](https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hunyuan3D-2.1)
- [IBM — Generative AI](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/generative-ai)

# What is code generation using AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-codegeneratie

> Code generation allows a model to suggest, extend or adapt software code. The real value lies in the proposal fitting the existing project and being able to be implemented in a controlled manner.

### In brief

Code generation means that a model creates code based on a task and available project information. This could be a function, test, script or modification to existing software. The model generates a proposal; the development environment determines how you implement that proposal. Code that looks good is not necessarily correct. Functionality, alignment with the project and maintainability are assessed through appropriate tests and reviews.

### What does the model require?

Describe the task the code is intended to perform, the input and output associated with the function, and any constraints that apply. Existing files, interfaces, tests and libraries used provide important context. A model that is unaware of the project requirements may produce a solution that appears logical in itself but does not fit the context. You should therefore provide specific information from the codebase rather than just a general request for a complete application.

### What is the difference between this and a coding model or agent?

A coding model is the model used for coding work. Code generation is a task performed by that model. A coding agent can also use tools to view files, apply changes and initiate checks. This combination enables a more comprehensive workflow, but does not automatically determine which permissions are appropriate. It remains useful to keep track of what is proposed, changed and actually carried out.

### A practical example

A developer wishes to extend an import function with a new data field. The model is provided with the existing function, sample input and relevant tests. It proposes a minor change and an additional test. The checks are then carried out and the change is assessed. Questions regarding missing input and existing records form part of that assessment. The process centres on a clearly defined modification, so that consequences and errors can be more easily identified.

### Which errors do you want to identify early on?

A model may use a non-existent function, miss an edge case or misinterpret existing rules. Furthermore, a test written by the same model may adopt the same assumption. You should therefore also assess whether the test verifies the desired behaviour. For integrations, error handling, permissions and input validation are all factors to consider. The relevant check depends on the change: a minor text adjustment requires a different approach to code that modifies data.

### How do you keep the work efficient?

Let the software locate files, select search results and carry out routine checks. Then provide the model with the context required for the next step. Sending the entire codebase each time can result in an unnecessary number of tokens and lead to delays. Compare models based on the specific tasks in your project, including rectification work. Good code generation helps a developer move forward and clearly shows which work still needs to be checked.

- [Mistral — Code and development tools](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/overview)
- [Hugging Face — Text generation with LLMs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/llm_tutorial)

# How does generation work with diffusion models?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/hoe-werkt-generatie-met-diffusion-modellen

> Many generative image models construct an image through successive steps starting from noise. What roles do the model, the prompt and the settings play during that process?

### In brief

A diffusion model learns how a coherent image can emerge from a distorted representation. Image generation often begins with random noise. The model then calculates successive processing steps, with a prompt guiding the outcome. This is how an image is created. This explanation concerns diffusion; not every generative model uses exactly this process. Text generation using a language model, for example, typically works by predicting subsequent tokens.

### What does the model learn during training?

A simplified explanation is that training images are corrupted with varying amounts of noise. The model learns how to reduce this corruption. During use, this knowledge is applied to build a new output from a noisy starting point. The precise prediction and calculation depend on the model and the chosen method. This is not a matter of removing a filter from a saved photo, but of producing a newly calculated result.

### How does text provide context for the image?

A text encoder converts the description into a representation that the generation process can use. The image model processes this information during the successive steps. In many pipelines, this takes place in a compact, latent space rather than directly on all image pixels. A decoder converts the final representation into an image. As a result, image generation often consists of several cooperating components rather than a single calculation.

### What do the steps and guidance involve?

The number of steps determines how often the pipeline performs an operation. More steps generally require more computation, but do not necessarily result in infinitely better quality. A scheduler determines how the successive steps are computed. For supported models, ‘Guidance’ controls the weighting of the task. A higher value does not automatically mean a better result. Settings must be appropriate for the model and the task; values from different models are not necessarily comparable.

### What is a seed in generation?

A seed determines the randomised start within the environment being used. Using the same seed allows you to compare variants more effectively whilst keeping other settings constant. This is useful if you wish to evaluate a single change to the command. It does not mean that the same number will produce exactly the same image on a different model, different hardware or a different software version. To ensure reproducibility, you should also record the model version, settings and the other components of the pipeline.

### What does this mean in practical terms?

Start with a specific task and assess which settings produce usable results. If necessary, work with a smaller format first to explore the composition, and only then move on to the final format. Editing a selected area may be more appropriate than having an entire image regenerated. Keep track of how many attempts and editing steps are required. This allows you to assess the speed and costs of the entire image workflow rather than just a single generation.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Components of a diffusion pipeline](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/quicktour)
- [Hugging Face — Text-to-image](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/using-diffusers/conditional_image_generation)
- [Hugging Face — Reproducible generation](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/using-diffusers/reusing_seeds)

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# AI generation locally or via an API?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/ai-generatie-lokaal-of-via-een-api

> Text, images and other output can sometimes be generated on your own hardware or produced via an external model service. Which approach best suits your data, desired quality and intended use?

### In brief

Local generation means that the model runs on your own device or server. With an external model API, you send a request to a service that carries out the processing. These are choices regarding the execution environment. An API can also point to your own local server: API means an interface, not necessarily the cloud. When weighing up your options, you must therefore be clear about where the model runs and what data leaves the environment.

### Which models can you run yourself?

You will need model files that you are authorised to use, suitable output software and sufficient computing power and memory. A freely downloadable model is not automatically open source or suitable for every application. Furthermore, the required capacity varies significantly between text, images, audio and video. Consider the specific task, output length and the number of concurrent users. This provides more guidance than simply a general description such as a large or small AI computer.

### When might an external approach be appropriate?

An external service can provide access to a model that you cannot run yourself, as well as additional features or capacity for variable usage. This comes with certain dependencies, such as connectivity, availability and the terms and conditions for data processing. Limits and waiting times may also affect the workflow. An external route is therefore a deliberate choice for a specific task, not automatically the best option for all data and all steps.

### How do you compare the actual costs?

For in-house hardware, purchase, energy, management and utilisation are all taken into account. For external services, the rate may, for example, be calculated per token, image, minute of audio, video clip or computing time. Also factor in failed attempts, regeneration and post-processing. A route with a low price per request can prove expensive if a large number of requests are required. Compare the total costs per usable end result based on your expected usage.

### Can you combine local and external services?

Yes, different steps can follow different execution paths. Code can first retrieve and structure data. A local model can prepare a draft, after which an external route is chosen for a specific additional task. Alternatively, all model processing remains local whilst a standard API supplies business data. Define what information each step receives. A combination remains manageable only if the division of tasks, data flows and exceptions are clear.

### How do you choose a suitable setup?

Use a small selection of representative projects to compare quality, turnaround time, correction work and costs. Determine which processing should remain local and how much management you wish to handle yourself. Also test whether the implementation is suitable for the expected number of users. Then choose a model route for each task and ensure the integration remains interchangeable where possible. In this way, you base your decision on practical use and control, rather than on a single impressive demonstration.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Memory usage of generative models](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/optimization/memory)
- [Hugging Face — Text generation with LLMs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/llm_tutorial)
- [Mistral — Code and development tools](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/overview)

# What are frontier models?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-zijn-frontier-modellen

> Frontier models are at the cutting edge of what AI is currently capable of. What does that say about quality, and when do you really need such a model?

### In brief

A frontier model is an AI model that is currently among the most advanced and capable models available. ‘Frontier’ means boundary or vanguard. It is not a fixed quality mark, nor is it a specific architecture: what is at the forefront today may be overtaken later. These are often versatile models capable of handling multiple types of complex tasks.

### What makes a model a ‘frontier’ model?

This concerns capabilities such as following complex instructions, solving problems, writing code or combining text and images. A model may excel at one task but be less effective at another. A high overall benchmark score therefore does not necessarily indicate how well it understands your Dutch documents or carries out your business processes.

### ‘Frontier’, ‘open’ and ‘local’ are distinct concepts

‘Frontier’ describes the capabilities. ‘Open’ or ‘closed’ refers to access and usage rights. Whether locally or via an external API refers to where the model is run. These characteristics do not automatically coincide. A local model is not necessarily simple, and a ‘Frontier’ model does not necessarily have to be closed. The available hardware and licence partly determine what is practically possible.

### A practical example

Suppose you want to categorise incoming messages into five categories and then work out the tricky exceptions. For the first step, you can test a small model. Only the complex messages are sent to a more powerful model. This is a possible workflow, not a proven performance claim. You compare the results against the same examples and clear acceptance criteria.

### When does a more powerful model make sense?

A more robust model can add value if errors are costly or the task requires a great deal of context and judgement. It may also mean longer waiting times or higher costs. You should therefore assess how many usable results you get, how much correction work is required and how data is processed. A model name or popularity alone is not a selection criterion.

### AITJE’s perspective on this

Start with the task and test different models on the same input. For each component, choose sufficient quality, with appropriate costs and control. Sometimes a frontier API is suitable, sometimes a model running on your own hardware, and sometimes a combination. By keeping that choice separate from the rest of your workflow, you can more easily deploy a different model later on.

## Sources

- [NCSC — What is meant by frontier AI?](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/advice-guidance/all-topics/frontier-ai)
- [RouteLLM — Research into model routing and the trade-off between quality and cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665)

# What are open-source AI models?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-zijn-open-source-ai-modellen

> Open source, open weights and free access do not mean the same thing. Find out what you can download, customise and run yourself — and what rights you need to do so.

### In brief

With an open-source AI model, the focus is on the freedom to use, examine, adapt and share the system. Simply offering a free chatbot or downloadable model files does not, in itself, make a model fully open source. In discussions about AI, the term is used broadly; therefore, look at what is actually available and what the licence permits.

### What are open weights?

‘Open weights’ means that the trained model parameters are available. This may allow you to run and customise the model yourself. However, the licence may contain restrictions, for example regarding certain applications or distribution. Furthermore, ‘open weights’ does not automatically imply that the training code and sufficient information about the training data are available. The OSI definition sets out broader requirements for an open AI system.

### How does this differ from a closed API?

With a closed API, you send a request to a service that runs the model for you. You receive the response, but usually not the weights or the ability to manage the same model version independently. A provider may also offer an API for a model with weights available. Access to files and access to a service are therefore different matters.

### A practical example

An organisation wishes to make its internal manuals searchable. With a suitable model and appropriate licence, it can set up the processing on its own server. This also involves a search index, access rights and a user interface. The model download is one component of that solution. Managing these components takes time, even if the download itself is free of charge.

### ‘Open’ does not automatically mean secure or free

Available weights do not provide any definitive information about answer quality, the origin of training data or the security of your installation. Running the system yourself entails costs for hardware, electricity and management. You should also check whether the licence terms are suitable for your application. A local model with online search tools may still send data to external services.

### What does this mean for your choice?

For a selected model, retain the version, licence and configuration. Test with your own tasks and clarify which components you can replace independently. In that case, openness becomes a practical way to maintain control, rather than just an attractive label. The choice between running the system yourself and using a service remains dependent on capacity, knowledge and usage.

## Sources

- [Open Source Initiative — Open Source AI Definition 1.0](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition)
- [Hugging Face — Fine-tuning](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/training)

# What are tokens in AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-zijn-tokens

> A language model works with tokens: small building blocks of input and output. They help determine how much context fits, how long a response takes and what an API request costs.

### In brief

A token is a unit used by a language model to process input and generate output. In the case of text, it can be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or another combination of characters. The tokeniser splits the input and assigns numbers to the segments. Tokens in this sense are not a cryptocurrency and are not separate subscription credits.

### A token is not the same as a word

The number of tokens in a sentence depends on the tokeniser and the text. A long Dutch compound word may be split into several parts. Code and numbers may be split differently from running text. A fixed ratio between words and tokens is therefore, at best, an estimate. For an accurate count, use the tokeniser or usage report of the chosen model.

### Input tokens and output tokens

Input tokens comprise the information provided to the model, such as instructions, conversation history and retrieved documents. Output tokens are the generated content. APIs may apply different rates for input, output, reused context and any reasoning tokens. Check the actual billing for the service used, even if you only see a short answer.

### A calculation example

For the purposes of this explanation, let’s assume that input costs €4 per million tokens. In that case, 100,000 input tokens would cost €0.40. This is a fictitious rate and only covers the input portion: output, additional requests and other costs may be added on top of this. If you resubmit the same large documents at every step, that input portion can quickly add up.

### Use fewer tokens without losing any information

Have the code remove duplicate fields, perform calculations and retrieve relevant data in advance. A search step can select the necessary passages, so that the model does not have to process the entire archive every time. Do, however, check that the selected information is sufficient. An assignment that is too brief may lead to errors and the need for additional attempts, which could ultimately make the final result more expensive.

### What does this mean for local AI?

A local model also processes tokens, although you do not need to receive an external token invoice. Input length and response length affect computational load, memory usage and latency. For both APIs and in-house hardware, measure the costs and quality per completed task. The cheapest token is not automatically the cheapest usable result.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Tokenisers and text segmentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/tokenizer_summary)
- [Hugging Face — Text generation with LLMs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/llm_tutorial)

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# What is model routing?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-modelrouting

> With model routing, a workflow selects which AI model will carry out a task. This allows you to combine local models and external APIs based on quality, data and costs.

### In brief

Model routing is the process of forwarding an AI request to a suitable model according to agreed criteria. The choice may depend on the type of task, the sensitivity of the data, the required quality or available capacity. A router may use simple rules or be a model in its own right. It is therefore part of the workflow, not a new language model.

### Why not use the same model for everything?

Different models have different strengths. A task such as message categorisation may require a different approach to complex code analysis. You do not necessarily have to use the most powerful model for every step. Research into routing shows that costs and quality can be optimised together; however, you must measure the outcome of your process yourself.

### A practical example

A possible order workflow first has the code retrieve customer data. A small model converts the email into agreed fields. If mandatory data is missing, the order is held up. Only ambiguous exceptions are passed on to a more sophisticated model or a member of staff. The router determines the route, whilst the checks prevent an incomplete order from proceeding automatically.

### Establishing rules and limits

Determine which data may be sent to an external API and which tasks must remain local. Also agree on what happens in the event of a fault, an invalid response or a budget being exceeded. An alternative route must not circumvent data policies. In such a situation, an error message or human assessment may be a better next step than automatically trying elsewhere.

### How do you know if the routing is working?

Compare different approaches to the same representative tasks. Take into account successful outcomes, corrections, waiting times and all requests. A cheaper model that has to retry regularly may end up costing more. Also keep track of why a particular route was chosen. This will allow you to see which exceptions are being forwarded too often and where a better rule is needed.

### What does this mean for AITJE?

In token management and optimisation, model routing can form part of a broader approach. First, you break the task down into smaller parts and make the input more specific; then you compare models. This way, you focus on a usable end result whilst ensuring the choice of model remains interchangeable. Whether the solution operates locally, at the edge or via frontier APIs depends on the requirements of the task.

## Sources

- [RouteLLM — Research into model routing and the trade-off between quality and cost](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18665)
- [Hugging Face — Tool usage and function calls](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/chat_extras)

# What is quantisation in AI models?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-quantisatie

> Quantisation stores model data with lower precision. As a result, a model may require less memory, but the impact on speed and quality varies depending on the application.

### In brief

Quantisation means that numbers in an AI model are represented with less precision. As a result, they take up less space. In the case of LLMs, this often involves model weights, but other calculations and stored intermediate results can also be quantised. The aim is to make the application runnable with less memory and appropriate computational effort.

### What do ‘16-bit’, ‘8-bit’ and ‘4-bit’ mean?

Bits are the units in which a number is stored. Fewer bits offer fewer possible values. A method must therefore determine how the original numbers are approximated. A model with 4-bit weights is not simply four times smaller than the full 16-bit installation: additional scaling data, software and the memory required for context also need to be taken into account.

### A comparison to help you understand

Consider rounding a measured value with many decimal places down to fewer decimal places. For some applications, this makes little difference; for others, the loss of precision is significant. This is a simplified comparison. Quantisation uses various techniques to minimise error and retain important information as effectively as possible.

### Why is this useful for local AI?

A model that does not fit into the available memory in its original form may still be usable in a different version. This can increase the choice of models on a Mac, PC or server. At the same time, you must reserve space for input, ongoing conversations and the KV cache. Therefore, file size alone does not determine whether the application will run smoothly.

### What might you be contributing?

Quality may vary, for example when dealing with precise instructions, calculations or less common languages. Speed improvements are also not guaranteed: these depend on hardware and support within the execution software. You should therefore test the actual implementation using the same questions and documents. In particular, check whether errors occur in the areas that are important for your work.

### Making a practical choice

Record the model version, quantisation and software used. Compare quality, memory and latency based on the expected number of users. Then choose the configuration that meets your requirements. A small file size in itself is not the aim; a stable application with sufficient quality and capacity is.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Quantisation overview](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/quantization/overview)
- [Hugging Face — KV cache and caching strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/kv_cache)

# What is fine-tuning?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-fine-tuning

> Fine-tuning further trains an existing model using targeted examples. When is this helpful, and when are a better prompt or document search function sufficient?

### In brief

Fine-tuning involves further training an existing model on a targeted set of examples. You don’t start from scratch: the model has already learnt general patterns. Through additional training, you aim to improve its behaviour for a specific task, style or domain. In doing so, the model’s weights are adjusted or additional trainable components are utilised.

### What sort of behaviour can you adjust?

Think about organising messages according to your own categories, always using the same response format, or better completing certain types of code. The examples illustrate the desired relationship between input and output. Fine-tuning does not guarantee that the model will apply all business rules without error. Rules that must be strictly adhered to are best checked using standard software as well.

### Fine-tuning is different from retrieving documents

With RAG, you search for relevant information and provide it in response to a query. Fine-tuning involves changing model behaviour through training. For up-to-date prices, staff details and manuals, fetching data is often the easiest way to keep information current. The two techniques can be combined: a customised model can provide answers based on information from a search function.

### A practical example

A support team always uses the same eight categories. First, test a clear prompt with a few examples. If the classification is not sufficiently consistent with this and there are enough well-labelled messages, you can investigate fine-tuning. Set aside a separate test set. This allows you to assess whether the model also works on messages it did not encounter during training.

### What are adapters and LoRA?

With some methods, you train small additional components rather than all the original weights. Such adapters can reduce the training resources required. LoRA is a well-known technique for this. This makes training more accessible, but the quality remains dependent on the examples and evaluation. Furthermore, an adapter must be compatible with the model version for which it was created.

### When is it worth it?

Compare the improvement with the costs of preparing, training, testing and maintaining data. First, try to see whether a more clearly defined task, prompt or search step is sufficient. Use fine-tuning only when that extra effort resolves a demonstrable problem. In doing so, retain the data rights, versions and test results used, so that any subsequent changes remain verifiable.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Fine-tuning](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/training)
- [Hugging Face — Parameter-efficient fine-tuning](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/peft)

# What is tool calling?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-tool-calling

> With tool calling, a language model can suggest calling a function. Your software retrieves data or performs an action, within the permissions you set yourself.

### In brief

Tool calling, also known as function calling, allows a model to make a structured request to use an available function. Examples include checking stock levels, performing a calculation or searching for a document. The model determines which function and input seem appropriate. The application checks that request and then decides whether to execute the function.

### The model does not execute the code itself

You describe which functions are available and which fields they expect. The model generates a call, often in a structured format. Your software does the actual work and returns the result. This way, the calculation remains in the code and the current stock levels remain in the stock management system. This is a different mechanism to asking the model to guess an answer based on its training.

### A practical example

An employee asks how many units of an item are available. The model submits a stock enquiry with an item number. The application checks access rights, requests the current stock levels from the system and returns only the relevant fields. The model then formulates a clear response. If an item number is missing, the workflow may first request clarification.

### Why does this help with token optimisation?

A function can retrieve specific data rather than sending an entire data set. Fixed calculations and format checks can also take place outside the model. As a result, the model has less unnecessary input. Tool descriptions, results and additional model runs also require context and time. Therefore, measure the entire chain, not just the first call.

### Rights are associated with the application

A tool request does not constitute consent. The executing software must verify user rights, input and permitted actions. Checking stock requires different permissions to placing an order. For actions with consequences, you can incorporate an explicit confirmation. Furthermore, return a clear error message if a tool does not work, so that the model does not have to assume a successful outcome.

### How does this relate to agents and MCP?

An agent can use multiple tool calls to carry out a task. MCP provides a common way of making tools and resources available to an AI application. Tool calling also works without MCP and does not automatically turn a standalone chatbot into an independent agent. The workflow determines how much freedom of choice the model actually has.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Tool usage and function calls](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/chat_extras)
- [Model Context Protocol — Architecture and components](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture)
