# What is MCP, the Model Context Protocol?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-mcp

> MCP provides AI applications with a unified way of accessing tools and information sources. What does this make easier, and what do you still need to sort out yourself?

### In brief

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It is an open protocol for connecting AI applications with tools and information sources. It describes how these components advertise their capabilities and exchange requests. This means that not every connection needs to use its own interface language from scratch. MCP itself is not a language model, database or search engine.

### Which components work together?

An AI application acts as the host. Within it, a client maintains the connection to an MCP server. This server is software that offers various functions, such as document searches or data retrieval. A server can run locally or be accessible via a network. The word ‘server’ here does not necessarily refer to a separate physical computer.

### Tools, resources and prompts

MCP distinguishes, amongst other things, between tools for executable functions, resources for available information and prompts for reusable instructions. The host determines how these capabilities are used within the application. A protocol governs the exchange; it does not determine which model provides the best answer or how your company should carry out a work process.

### A practical example

An internal assistant must be able to search through manuals. You can set up an MCP server that offers a search function and returns only those documents to which the employee has access. A suitable AI application can discover and utilise that function. The underlying document archive remains in place; MCP acts as a link to that source, not a replacement for the archive.

### What do you still need to sort out yourself?

You remain responsible for access rights, reliable tools and what the application is permitted to do with the results. A local MCP server can, in turn, access external systems. Connecting locally does not, therefore, automatically mean that all data remains local. For each connection, specify where processing takes place and what information the user and the model actually receive.

### When is MCP suitable?

It can be useful when multiple suitable AI applications need to use the same sources or functions. For a single, simple connection, a standard API may suffice. Choose based on supported functions and management, not because the protocol is popular. Also check the supported protocol versions before considering a connection to be interchangeable.

## Sources

- [Model Context Protocol — Architecture and components](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture)
- [Hugging Face — Tool usage and function calls](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/chat_extras)

# What are AI hallucinations?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-zijn-ai-hallucinaties

> AI can provide a convincing answer that is factually incorrect. Learn how to recognise fabricated information and build applications that handle uncertainty more effectively.

### In brief

An AI hallucination is generated content that is incorrect, fabricated or unsubstantiated, even though the response may sound reliable. Examples include a non-existent source, an incorrect amount or a software function that does not exist at all. The term describes an error in the output; it does not imply that the model possesses human perception or conscious intent.

### Why is this happening?

A language model generates appropriate output based on learnt patterns and the available context. This process is not an automatic fact-check. Missing information, unclear questions or incorrect sources may lead to a plausible but inaccurate response. Even with sufficient context, the model may misinterpret passages or mix up information from different sources.

### A practical example

An employee asks about the notice period in a contract. The document contains no provision on this matter. A poorly configured assistant enters a standard notice period as if it were taken from the contract. A better-configured application states that the provision has not been found, shows what has been consulted and refers the query for assessment.

### Does this help with searching within your own documents?

RAG can add relevant source information, meaning the model needs to rely less on its general training to supplement its output. However, even then, the wrong documents may be found or source passages may be misrepresented. Where possible, show the passage used and the document version. A source reference is only useful if you can verify whether the source actually supports the conclusion.

### What checks can you add?

Have the model identify any missing data and limit the response to the available information when the task requires it. Check amounts and mandatory fields against the code. Use test questions where the correct answer is known, including questions that cannot be answered. For important decisions, a proper assessment remains necessary, even if previous answers were correct.

### What does this mean for AITJE?

A local installation does not prevent hallucinations. Quality depends on model selection, data provision and checks. You should therefore build an application around a clear task and a recognisable boundary: when can the system respond, when must it stop, and who is monitoring it at that point? Reliability also involves handling a query for which no substantiated answer is available in the right way.

## Sources

- [Anthropic — Reducing hallucinations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations)
- [Research — Code hallucinations and API documentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09726)

# What is digital sovereignty?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-digitale-soevereiniteit

> Digital sovereignty is about having control over your data, systems and choices. In the context of AI, this also encompasses model access, management and the ability to switch providers.

### In brief

Digital sovereignty is about having control over digital systems, data and the conditions under which you use them. For an organisation, this means, amongst other things, being able to determine who has access, where processing takes place and how to switch suppliers. It is not the same as building everything yourself or never using an external service.

### Why is this relevant to AI?

An AI application can utilise knowledge from documents, customer data and business processes. If the application is entirely dependent on a single external API, changes to models, terms and conditions or availability may affect your work. The key question is which dependencies you are prepared to accept and which components you can manage or replace yourself. This requires an understanding of the entire chain.

### A Dutch location is one component

Having a server in the Netherlands may be important, but does not in itself guarantee full control. Management rights, contracts, the software used and any external connections also play a part. Conversely, an external service may be part of a deliberate choice offering good export options. You must assess both the location and the ability to act independently.

### A practical example

An organisation stores its documents in its own environment and uses a replaceable model layer. A local model answers internal queries. For a different task, an authorised external service can be used without moving the document archive. This is one possible setup: the benefits depend on access rights, data flows and how well a transition has actually been prepared.

### Which questions would be helpful?

Can you export data and configuration? Can you continue to use an older model version? Who can manage the systems if the supplier fails? What will continue to work without an external connection? Answer these questions with documentation and a brief practical test. A promise that something is independent is less useful than a demonstrable ability to continue working or to migrate.

### The link to AITJE

Running AI on your own hardware or server can be a way to retain greater control. This entails responsibilities for updates, security and business continuity. You should therefore opt for a feasible setup with clearly defined roles. The aim is to enable you to use and replace the technology in an informed manner, whilst ensuring the application continues to support your work.

## Sources

- [Central Government — Vision for digital autonomy and sovereignty](https://www.rijksoverheid.nl/documenten/2025/12/18/bijlage-2-visie-digitale-autonomie-en-soevereiniteit-van-de-overheid)
- [CMA — Research into competition and switching between cloud services](https://www.gov.uk/cma-cases/cloud-services-market-investigation)

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# What is ablation in language models?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-abliteration

> Abliteration adjusts a model’s internal properties to reduce learned rejection behaviour. What does this change, and what does it not tell us about the quality?

### In brief

Abliteration is an informal term for techniques that aim to reduce a language model’s refusal behaviour by adjusting internal model representations or weights. You often see the term used in connection with modified models where the weights are available. The standard spelling is abliteration. It is not a standard quality mark, nor is it a guarantee that a model will carry out every task from now on.

### Where did the idea come from?

Researchers found an internal bias in the chat models studied that was strongly correlated with the refusal of certain requests. By influencing that bias, the refusal behaviour changed. Abliteration builds on insights of this kind. This describes a finding relating to specific models and experiments; it does not prove that every model reacts in the same way.

### What is the difference between this and a prompt or fine-tuning?

A prompt provides instructions during use. Fine-tuning further trains a model using examples. Ablation attempts to modify an internal pattern in a more targeted way, sometimes by creating a modified version of the weights. The outcome depends on the technique and the original model. It is therefore more than simply a request to respond differently in a chat.

### Fewer rejections do not automatically mean better responses

A model that provides answers more frequently can still make mistakes, invent something or follow an instruction incorrectly. The adjustment does not add any new reliable knowledge. Other characteristics may also change. You should therefore assess a modified version against the actual task, including factual accuracy and the ability to recognise missing information.

### A practical example

Suppose your model rejects a legitimate technical document query too often. First, investigate which instruction, document context or application filter is causing this. A different prompt, model choice or configuration may resolve the issue. A customised model version is a separate option that you should compare using the same test questions; a general promise of fewer limitations says little about that specific problem.

### What does this mean for a business environment?

Permissions within an application, access control to files and rules governing actions remain necessary, regardless of the model’s rejection behaviour. When using a customised model, specify which version and modification you are using. Make your choice based on measurable task suitability. AITJE can only deploy a model meaningfully within a workflow if the information, permissions and controls are also appropriate.

## Sources

- [Arditi et al. — Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11717)
- [Hugging Face — Fine-tuning](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/training)

## Contact

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# What are the weights of an AI model?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-zijn-model-weights

> Weights are the trained numbers that determine how a model processes information. Find out how model weights, parameters and a downloadable model file are related.

### In brief

Weights, or model weights, are numbers in a neural network that influence how input is converted into output. During training, these numbers are adjusted to improve performance on training examples. During normal use of a language model, the weights usually remain the same. The model uses them in conjunction with the information from the current prompt.

### Why are they called ‘weights’?

A weight determines how heavily a component of a calculation is factored in. A simple equation is a formula in which different characteristics each have their own multiplication factor. An LLM involves much more complex, sequential calculations. The meaning is spread across large numbers of weights; there isn’t a single, recognisable box for every fact that you can open and edit.

### What do 7B or 70B parameters mean?

The B stands for billion. A designation such as 7B usually refers to approximately seven billion model parameters. The number gives an indication of scale, but does not fully predict the quality for your specific task. Architecture, training data and further training also play a part. Furthermore, with some models, not all parameters are used simultaneously for every token.

### What is included in a model download?

Model weights are stored in files. To run a language model, you also need suitable output software, model configuration and a tokeniser. The precision with which the weights are stored affects how much space they take up. Quantisation allows you to adjust this storage requirement. The memory required for running requests and the KV cache is in addition to the memory required for the weights.

### A practical example

You can test the same model version in different configurations, for example with weights set to higher or lower precision. These configurations may have different memory requirements and produce different results. A download may fit on your hard drive, whilst the application may not fit properly into your working memory. You should therefore also test with real documents and the intended number of concurrent users.

### What does ‘access to weights’ mean?

Available weights allow you to run the model yourself, provided the hardware, software and licence permit it. This does not mean that all training data is public or that there are no restrictions on use. Record the version and rights. This way, you know which model you are managing and can later compare any change in behaviour with the original version.

## Sources

- [Google Machine Learning Crash Course — Weights in a model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/linear-regression)
- [Hugging Face — Quantisation overview](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/quantization/overview)
- [Open Source Initiative — Open Source AI Definition 1.0](https://opensource.org/ai/open-source-ai-definition)

# What is KV-cache in an LLM?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-kv-cache

> The KV cache stores intermediate results from a language model, so that it does not have to repeat as much work during text generation. This helps with speed, but also requires memory.

### In brief

KV here stands for key and value: two types of internal vectors that a transformer uses during attention. Attention helps the model process connections with previous input. The KV cache stores previously calculated keys and values so that they can be reused for the next token. In this LLM context, therefore, it does not refer to a general key-value database.

### Why does that make a difference?

A language model typically constructs a response step by step. The next token depends in part on the previous tokens. Without reuse, it would have to recalculate many earlier intermediate results each time. The cache eliminates the need for some of that repetitive work. It is an optimisation of the model’s execution, not additional training.

### The cache also uses memory

More retained context and more concurrent requests may require more cache memory. Exactly how much depends, amongst other things, on the architecture and the chosen caching strategy. Some models only retain a limited window in certain layers. A model file that fits into memory is therefore not enough: there must also be sufficient space for the active requests.

### A practical example

A local assistant handles short queries smoothly. With a long document or multiple users at the same time, the same machine is more likely to become overloaded. The weights have not increased, but more working memory is required to handle the requests. You may then, for example, need to run fewer conversations simultaneously or select the context more carefully. You will need to test which solution works best on that particular installation.

### KV-cache is not a permanent personal memory

The cache contains internal interim results for a specific context. It is not a standard list of facts and does not automatically alter the model weights. Saving conversation history, reusing repeated prompt sections and managing personal knowledge are other functions. Whilst they may be technically related, they should not all be described as the same type of memory in a user promise.

### What does this mean for your setup?

Allocate capacity for model weights and context. Test latency and memory usage based on the number of users and document lengths you anticipate. There are various caching techniques, such as reduced precision or relocation to different memory. These can save space, but may also cause delays or differences in quality. You should therefore choose based on your specific workload.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — KV cache and caching strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/kv_cache)
- [Hugging Face — How caching works](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/cache_explanation)

# What is a vector in AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-vector

> A vector is an ordered sequence of numbers. In AI, such a sequence helps to represent, compare and retrieve information — for example, when searching by meaning.

### In brief

A vector is an ordered sequence of numbers, such as [0.2; 0.8; -0.1]. Each number has a fixed position, a dimension. Vectors enable software to process information that originally consists of text, images or other data. A vector is the form of representation; the way in which you arrange those numbers determines what they mean.

### A simple comparison

You can describe a product using figures for weight, length and price. That way, you know exactly what each dimension means. AI vectors can have many more dimensions, with the characteristics being learnt collectively. Such a dimension is usually not easy to name, such as ‘topic’ or ‘tone’. The combination of numbers is what matters.

### What is the difference between this and an embedding?

An embedding is a learned representation of information, often in the form of a vector. An embedding model can place sentences with related meanings close together. Not every vector is therefore an embedding. Vectors are also used for other internal calculations, including the keys and values in the attention layers of a language model.

### How can you search for it?

A search application uses the same embedding model to create a vector from the query and from document passages. It then compares the vectors to find related passages. Different comparison methods measure that relationship in different ways. A high similarity score means that a passage is likely to be relevant; it is not proof that the passage is true or up to date.

### A practical example

Someone is looking for information on how to regain access. A user guide uses the words ‘reset password’. Searching by embeddings can help locate that passage, even without the exact same words. You then display the original passage with its source and date. The vector therefore does not replace the document, but helps to locate it.

### What do you need to set up properly?

Compare representations created for the same vector space. If you change the embedding model, re-indexing may be required. In addition, maintain document permissions and source information. A user should not be shown a confidential passage simply because it closely matches the query. For a useful search function, the text found and access control are at least as important as the vectors.

## Sources

- [Google Machine Learning Crash Course — Embedding space](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/embeddings/embedding-space)
- [Hugging Face — KV cache and caching strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/kv_cache)

# What is a token factory?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-token-factory

> A ‘token factory’ is a metaphor for infrastructure that produces AI output. What lies behind such a factory, and how does this relate to inference and costs?

### In brief

‘Token factory’ is a figure of speech for a system or platform that produces AI output at scale. The term is used in the context of AI factories and inference infrastructure. It is not a distinct type of language model, nor is it a universal technical standard. This article concerns tokens from AI models, not the creation of crypto tokens.

### What does such an environment consist of?

Models, computing hardware, memory, networks and software are required to process requests. This is supported by, amongst other things, data provision, access management and monitoring. NVIDIA uses AI Factory for a broader infrastructure that can also support training and other AI activities. Token Factory focuses primarily on the production of model output during operation.

### Why is it called a factory?

The analogy illustrates a chain: data and commands are received, calculations are performed, and usable output is sent to applications. Just as in a production process, there is capacity, queues and quality control. However, the word ‘factory’ says nothing about the quality of each response. More tokens produced can also mean more redundant text.

### A practical example

An organisation allows multiple internal applications to use the same model server. An assistant asks questions, a document workflow generates summaries and a developer has code explained. The platform allocates capacity and records usage. Even on a small scale, this can already constitute a shared AI facility; the term ‘factory’ does not automatically imply a large data centre.

### How do you assess capacity and costs?

Tokens per second can be useful, but do not indicate how many users receive a satisfactory result within the desired time. Also measure waiting time, utilisation and successful tasks. A machine that is left running all day for a few short queries may prove more cost-effective than the same machine with a constant workload. Electricity, purchase and management costs should therefore be included in the comparison.

### What suits ‘AITJE’?

Start with the tasks and the expected usage. For some organisations, a dedicated shared model server is suitable; for others, an API or a combination of both. Configure the input efficiently and route different tasks to suitable models. The aim is to achieve usable AI capacity with insight into usage and costs, not to generate as many tokens as possible for the sake of it.

- [NVIDIA — AI factories](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/solutions/ai-factories/)
- [NVIDIA — Building AI Factories for the Enterprise](https://docs.nvidia.com/enterprise-reference-architectures/white-paper/latest/building-ai-factories-for-the-enterprise.html)

# What is inference in an LLM?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-inference

> Inference is the process of using a trained model to produce an outcome. In the case of an LLM, this involves processing input and then constructing a response.

### In brief

Inference is the phase in which you use a trained AI model to produce a prediction or other outcome. With a language model, this could be an answer, a summary or a piece of code. The model performs calculations using the available weights and the current input. A normal chat does not automatically change those weights; training and using the model are separate processes.

### What happens during text generation?

First, the input is converted into the format expected by the model. In the case of an LLM, text consists of tokens. The model then processes the context and constructs the output. In many generative language models, this happens token by token. The selection of the next tokens also depends on settings that determine how predictable or varied the output may be.

### Prefill and decode

Prefill is the processing of the provided context before the next output is generated. Decode is the repeated generation of new tokens. A long input can increase the time to first response; a long reply requires additional generation work. The KV cache helps to reuse certain previous calculations during that process.

### A practical example

You are asking for a summary of a document. Processing the document text is part of inference, as is creating the summary. If you then ask a specific question, further calculations are required. Whether previous context is reused efficiently depends on the application. A saved chat does not automatically mean that all previous computational costs are eliminated.

### What does the speed depend on?

Model size, precision, hardware, input length and concurrent requests all play a part. A quick, short test therefore does not always predict how a team will perform with large documents. Measure the latency to the first token and the time to a fully usable response. Search steps and tool calls can also affect the total turnaround time.

### Locally and via an API

Inference can take place on your own device, on your own server or via an external provider. With an API, the user pays according to the terms of service; running it yourself entails hardware and management costs. The technical core remains the same: an existing model is used. Optimisation begins with a clear task, a specific context and an appropriate implementation.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Text generation with LLMs](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/llm_tutorial)
- [Hugging Face — KV cache and caching strategies](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/kv_cache)

# What is a vision model?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-vision-model

> A vision model processes visual information, such as photographs and document images. A vision-language model combines this with language to answer questions about an image.

### In brief

A vision model is an AI model for visual information. For example, it can classify images or recognise objects. A vision-language model combines images and language: you provide an image plus a question and receive a textual response. Not every vision model can chat, and not every language model can process images.

### What can you do with it?

Think of extracting data from an image of a document, explaining a graph or describing a photograph. Whether a model performs well depends on its training, the task and the quality of the input. Furthermore, video is a separate capability that not every image model supports. A product that accepts photos is therefore not automatically suitable for every visual application.

### How does this differ from OCR?

OCR focuses on recognising handwritten or printed text. A vision-language model can also answer questions about layout, objects and relationships within an image. For a fixed document task, an OCR step followed by standard code may be more suitable. You can also combine techniques, for example, text recognition for fields and a model for providing an explanation.

### A practical example

A technician submits a photograph and a brief note. A model can generate a conceptual description of the visible situation. The workflow then retrieves material prices from a database and allows a member of staff to check the proposed work. The model does not need to guess the prices from the photograph. This is a possible application; it is not a guarantee that every detail will be reliably recognised.

### What should you bear in mind?

Blurry images, small text and unclear details can lead to misinterpretations. Even an image model can convincingly describe something that is not visible. Therefore, leave missing or uncertain fields open for verification. Test using the actual types of photos and documents encountered in practice, including difficult and incomplete input.

### What does this mean for your AI environment?

Image processing may require more capacity and has its own usage limits. Also check where images are processed and whether personal data in the images is required for the task. Compare a local model, an external API and a combination of OCR, code and AI. The best approach depends on accuracy, data policy and the cost per verified result.

## Sources

- [Hugging Face — Multimodal models using text and images](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/v4.52.3/en/chat_templating_multimodal)
- [InternLM-XComposer-2.5 — Research into vision-language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.03320)

# What is a coding model?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-coding-model

> A coding model is designed for tasks involving software code. It can assist with explanations, additions and modifications, but a functioning development environment also requires tools and tests.

### In brief

A coding model is an AI model that is specifically suited to, or has been further trained for, programming tasks. It can complete code, provide explanations, investigate errors or suggest changes. General language models can also perform programming tasks. ‘Coding model’ therefore describes the task-specific nature of the model; it is not a guarantee that every generated change will work.

### What makes programming a special task?

Code must be compatible with a language, libraries, project structure and existing behaviour. A proposal may look convincing yet still use a non-existent function or overlook an important edge case. Good context therefore consists of relevant files, instructions and up-to-date documentation. Simply sending a large amount of source code is not the same as providing the correct information.

### A model and a coding agent are different

The model generates output. A coding agent also uses software to read files, apply changes and carry out checks. The permissions and development tools determine which actions are possible. A model with programming knowledge therefore does not automatically have access to your repository or permission to publish a change.

### A practical example

A developer requests that an error in order validation be rectified. The application provides the relevant code and the expected behaviour. The model suggests a change, after which the development environment runs appropriate tests. The developer assesses the outcome. If a test fails, that information is used to refine the change; a passing test result does not replace all substantive assessment.

### How do you choose a suitable model?

Test using your programming language and real project tasks. Compare the quality of changes, the level of guidance required and the time taken to achieve a usable result. Also consider integration with development tools and the ability to handle longer context. A model that performs well on a small puzzle may be less suitable for maintenance within a large existing codebase.

### What does this mean for AITJE Coder?

A dedicated coding environment can combine a model running on local hardware or a dedicated server with suitable tools. This offers different management and data options compared to running everything via an external API. External models can also be deliberately deployed when the task requires it. Ensure that code, development rights and model selection are organised in such a way that you can monitor changes and adapt your environment.

## Sources

- [Mistral — Coding with a model and development tools](https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/overview)
- [Research — Code hallucinations and API documentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09726)

# What is a VC subsidy for AI services?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-vc-subsidy

> Investors and temporary grants can finance growth before a service pays for itself. How might such a potential grant affect your view of AI costs?

### In brief

‘VC subsidy’ is an informal term for the benefit users may experience when investors finance a service’s growth and losses. VC stands for venture capital. It is not a fixed financial category, nor is it proof that every low-cost AI service operates at a loss. It refers to a possible funding dynamic, not a universal explanation for API prices.

### How can financing support a low price?

A company may raise capital to fund development, infrastructure and customer acquisition before revenue covers all those expenses. A supplier may also provide temporary credits or promotional credits. Investment funds and supplier credits are different forms of support. In both cases, part of the bill may temporarily fall outside the direct customer price.

### Why does a low token price prove very little?

A provider can operate efficiently, utilise existing capacity or offer a smaller model. Furthermore, operating loss is not the same as a loss on every API request: research costs and other expenditure also count towards this. Without suitable information on costs and revenue, you cannot determine the extent to which a specific service is subsidised. You should therefore not present assumptions as facts in this regard.

### A fictional example

Suppose a team receives temporary cloud credits for a trial. During that trial, a workflow appears to cost almost nothing. Once the credit has been used up, the standard usage charges apply. This example illustrates the difference between a temporary bill and ongoing costs. It says nothing about the profitability or future pricing of a particular AI provider.

### How should you handle this?

Carry out a calculation without taking temporary discounts into account and include all steps in the workflow. Also investigate how a different usage volume or a different model would affect the costs. You do not need to predict future price rises to do this. It is helpful simply to make the assumptions transparent and avoid locking in a model choice unnecessarily.

### What does this mean for AITJE?

Compare API usage and in-house infrastructure in terms of total costs and usable results. An in-house server requires purchase, power and management; an external service offers different economies of scale and dependencies. Let a pilot demonstrate what works and then assess the structural setup. A temporary low price can help you get started, but is not a complete business case.

## Sources

- [SEC — Financing and investors in private companies](https://www.sec.gov/resources-small-businesses/capital-raising-building-blocks/private-companies-sec)
- [AWS — Promotional cloud credits for start-ups](https://aws.amazon.com/startups/credits?lang=en-US)

# What is loss-leader pricing in the context of AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-loss-leader-pricing

> With loss-leader pricing, an offer is priced at a loss to attract customers. How does this differ from a temporary discount, finance options and predatory pricing?

### In brief

Loss-leader pricing is a pricing strategy whereby a product or service is offered below cost price to attract customers. The provider expects, for example, to recoup the investment through other purchases, add-ons or a longer-term customer relationship. You may also hear the term ‘loss-leader price’. This does not mean that every discount or free trial is automatically part of such a strategy.

### What might this look like in the context of AI?

Consider, as a possible scenario, low-cost API usage within a platform that also offers paid storage, management or larger packages. The price of a single component does not, therefore, tell the whole story about the total bill. To determine whether an offer is genuinely loss-making, you need insight into the relevant costs. The visible token price alone is insufficient for this.

### A fictional example

A hypothetical supplier offers a basic function temporarily below cost and expects to generate revenue from a paid management package. A user with only the basic function benefits initially. An organisation purchasing the full package must compare the total cost. This is an illustrative example of the mechanism, not a description of a specific provider or a prediction of price increases.

### The difference with VC subsidy

VC subsidy describes how capital can temporarily finance growth or losses. Loss-leader pricing describes the pricing strategy for an offer. These terms may occur together, but do not necessarily have to. For example, a larger, profitable company can afford a loss-making entry-level product from other sources of income without the involvement of venture capital.

### The difference from predatory pricing

Predatory pricing refers to an exclusionary pricing practice that undermines competition. A low or loss-making price alone does not prove this. For a legal assessment within the EU, factors such as market power, costs and the effect on competition are relevant. Loss-leader pricing should therefore not automatically be labelled as predatory pricing or unlawful conduct.

### What does this mean for your choice of AI?

Compare the entire workflow: model calls, storage, integrations, management and the effort involved in switching providers later on. Check whether trial prices and standard rates differ. A favourable introductory offer can be an excellent choice as long as you understand the terms and conditions. Keep your data and model links transferable wherever possible, so that you still have options even if your needs change.

## Sources

- [FTC — Predatory or Below-Cost Pricing (US context)](https://www.ftc.gov/advice-guidance/competition-guidance/guide-antitrust-laws/single-firm-conduct/predatory-or-below-cost-pricing)
- [European Commission — Article 102 and abuse of a dominant position](https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/antitrust-and-cartels/legislation/application-article-102-tfeu_en)

## Contact

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# What is predatory pricing, or price gouging?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-predatory-pricing

> Predatory pricing refers to low prices that can exclude competition. Why is a cheap AI API not in itself evidence of such a practice?

### In brief

Predatory pricing, often referred to as ‘predatory pricing’, is an exclusionary pricing practice whereby a company with a dominant position sets prices below the relevant costs in order to marginalise competitors or reduce competition. In the EU, this falls within the scope of the prohibition on the abuse of a dominant position. The concept is therefore more specific than simply a company selling at low prices or investing heavily.

### Why are low prices not proof in themselves?

Low prices may also result from more efficient production, economies of scale or simply competition. This can actually help users. When making an assessment, you should consider, amongst other things, the relevant market, dominant position, price-cost ratio and the circumstances surrounding the behaviour. You cannot draw that conclusion from a single API rate alone.

### The idea behind the term

The economic rationale is that a company temporarily forgoes revenue to weaken the competition, thereby leaving customers with fewer alternatives later on. Higher future prices may be a factor in this. A specific legal assessment requires more than this explanation; which facts and tests are decisive also depends on the applicable legal rules and circumstances.

### A fictional example

Two AI services charge different token prices. That merely indicates a price difference. Perhaps they use different models, hardware or terms of service. Without data on costs and market position, you cannot say that the cheapest service is engaging in predatory pricing. This example helps to distinguish between an observable rate and an unproven conclusion about the strategy behind it.

### Why is this relevant for organisations?

You don’t need to assess a competition case to understand your dependencies. An application that is heavily reliant on a single service may be vulnerable to changes in terms and conditions or availability, regardless of the justification for the price. You should therefore consider model replacement, export options and alternative routes. These are practical choices that you can explore yourself.

### What can you compare?

Calculate the costs per successful outcome, including all necessary steps. Set out the requirements that an alternative must meet and test a small-scale transition. Keep factual pricing information separate from assumptions about business operations. This will enable you to procure sensibly and design a workflow without resorting to unfounded accusations against suppliers.

## Sources

- [European Commission — Article 102 and abuse of a dominant position](https://competition-policy.ec.europa.eu/antitrust-and-cartels/legislation/application-article-102-tfeu_en)
- [FTC — Predatory or Below-Cost Pricing (US context)](https://www.ftc.gov/advice-guidance/competition-guidance/guide-antitrust-laws/single-firm-conduct/predatory-or-below-cost-pricing)

# What is vendor lock-in in AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-vendor-lock-in

> Vendor lock-in occurs when switching suppliers becomes difficult or expensive. With AI, this dependency often lies in data, APIs, model behaviour and workflows all at once.

### In brief

Vendor lock-in means that an organisation is so dependent on a supplier that switching becomes difficult, expensive or time-consuming. Switching costs are the costs involved in switching: money, development work, retesting and, in some cases, disruption to work. Lock-in does not necessarily involve deliberate deception. It can also develop as a convenient platform takes on an increasing number of tasks.

### Where does dependency arise with AI?

Not just when making an API call. Prompts, specific response formats, built-in search functions, saved files and model behaviour can also be vendor-specific. A different model may support the same technical interface yet still provide different responses. As a result, you may sometimes need not only to adjust the integration but also to reassess the entire task.

### A practical example

An assistant stores documents in a supplier-specific search environment and uses that platform’s own conversational features. Later, the organisation wishes to change the model. This will require document export, indexing, links and test questions. An export button for the original files is useful, but does not mean that all configuration and expected behaviour will be transferred.

### How can you minimise switching costs?

Store source data in a portable format and document key settings. Where possible, keep the model linkage separate from business logic. Create a test dataset with desired outcomes so that you can assess an alternative fairly. Open protocols can simplify integration, but do not automatically eliminate differences in model quality and platform features.

### Does running locally automatically mean there is no lock-in?

No. Even an in-house installation can be dependent on a single management provider, hardware platform or specialised software. You retain greater control when you have access to data, configuration and documentation, and when maintenance is transferable. An open model licence can help, but without management expertise and a feasible migration path, dependencies will remain.

### How does AITJE strike the right balance?

Not every dependency needs to be removed. A managed service can save a great deal of work. Do, however, be clear about which components you accept and which you wish to keep replaceable. A small trial with a second model or runtime environment can reveal just how much migration work is actually required. This allows you to assess your freedom of choice in terms of practical possibilities.

## Sources

- [CMA — Research into competition and switching between cloud services](https://www.gov.uk/cma-cases/cloud-services-market-investigation)
- [Central Government — Vision for digital autonomy and sovereignty](https://www.rijksoverheid.nl/documenten/2025/12/18/bijlage-2-visie-digitale-autonomie-en-soevereiniteit-van-de-overheid)
- [Model Context Protocol — Architecture and components](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/learn/architecture)

## Contact

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# What is an LLM?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-llm

> An LLM is a large language model that can understand, predict and generate text. It often seems intelligent, but the quality of the result depends heavily on context, model choice and how you use it.

### In brief

LLM stands for Large Language Model. It is a language model that has been trained on large amounts of text and can therefore recognise patterns in language. This enables it to answer questions, rewrite texts, summarise, classify and generate new text based on a prompt.

### What is an LLM good at?

LLMs excel at tasks centred on language. These include drafting draft emails, structuring notes, translating internal information into understandable language, or summarising documents. Their strength lies primarily in speed, linguistic sensitivity and flexibility.

### Where do things often go wrong?

An LLM does not reason like a human and does not automatically know what is true or up to date. The model can make convincing-sounding errors, invent information or provide overly general answers. That is why you must carefully consider the use of sources, checks and the intended purpose of the output.

### What does this mean for organisations?

For organisations, an LLM is only truly useful if it fits within a process. This is not just about the model itself, but also about context, rights, logging, security and whether the model runs locally or in the cloud. The business value lies in a reliable application, not in the demo alone.

### How can you use an LLM effectively?

Start with a clear task: for example, summarising, classifying or answering internal queries. Then add the relevant context and preconditions, and determine how staff will verify the outcome. In this way, you treat an LLM not as a magic box, but as a tool within a work process.

## Contact

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# What is edge AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-edge-ai

> Edge AI means that AI runs close to the source of the data, for example on a device, server or local network. This allows you to work faster and often gives you greater control over privacy, continuity and costs.

### In brief

With edge AI, you process data within or close to your own environment rather than sending everything to an external cloud. This can be done on the device itself, on a local server or on infrastructure within your own network. That is why edge AI is often also referred to as local AI.

### Why do organisations choose this?

The main reasons are speed, privacy, control over data and reduced reliance on external platforms. If a process needs to remain available at all times, or if sensitive information cannot simply be processed externally, edge AI often becomes an immediately attractive option.

### When does edge AI make sense?

Edge AI is particularly suitable for knowledge-based queries regarding internal documents, local assistants, production environments, healthcare settings or environments with unstable internet connections. Furthermore, where predictable costs and in-house infrastructure are important, running locally is often more attractive than a fully cloud-based approach.

### What do you need to organise in practice?

Local AI requires more than just hardware. You also need to consider updates, monitoring, access management, backups, logging and the question of which components are permitted to communicate externally and which are not. It is therefore an infrastructure choice with operational implications.

### Common misconception

Edge AI does not automatically mean that everything is better. Local deployment can offer many advantages, but it also requires management, technical decisions and clear boundaries. The right question is not whether the cloud is bad, but which part of a process belongs locally and which part may, if necessary, run externally.

# What is local AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-local-ai

> Local AI means that AI runs within your own environment, for example on a local device, server or network. It is about having greater control over data, availability, costs and dependence on external AI platforms.

### In brief

Local AI is AI that is not entirely dependent on an external cloud environment. Processing takes place locally, on the organisation’s own hardware or within its own network. This keeps the infrastructure closer to the organisation using the AI.

### Why is this relevant?

Much AI usage takes place via external platforms involving subscriptions, API charges and third-party rules. Local AI reduces that dependency. This is particularly beneficial when internal expertise, privacy, continuity or predictable costs are important.

### Is local AI the same as edge AI?

The terms overlap significantly. Edge AI emphasises that processing takes place close to the data source. Local AI emphasises that the AI is available within your own environment. In practice, the terms are often used interchangeably.

### What can you do locally?

This includes answering internal queries, searching through documents, using knowledge bases, creating summaries, running agents or supporting workflows. Not everything needs to be hosted locally, but components involving sensitive data or requiring high availability can often benefit greatly from it.

### What should you bear in mind?

Local AI requires sound decisions regarding hardware, models, access, updates and management. It is not a one-off solution, but an infrastructure choice. The best solution combines local capabilities with clear agreements on what, if anything, may still be outsourced.

# What is on-premises AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-on-premise-ai

> On-premise AI means that AI runs on infrastructure managed by your own organisation or at your own premises. This can help with privacy, compliance, business continuity and control over systems.

### In brief

On-premises AI runs on hardware belonging to the organisation, branch or in-house management environment. Rather than sending all processing to an external AI service, you keep the most important components closer to your own infrastructure.

### When should you choose this option?

On-premises AI makes sense when data is sensitive, systems need to continue operating locally, or when external platforms do not align with policy, costs or availability. It is particularly relevant for organisations with clear requirements regarding management and access.

### What is the difference between this and cloud AI?

With cloud AI, processing largely runs on infrastructure provided by an external provider. With on-premises AI, more responsibility lies with the organisation itself or with a partner managing the local environment. You gain control, but must organise management effectively.

### What components are included?

In addition to the model, you’ll need hardware, software, access management, logging, updates, monitoring and support arrangements. On-premises AI is therefore not just about installing a model, but about building a workable environment.

### Practical nuance

‘On-premise’ does not mean that nothing can ever be outsourced. Some organisations combine on-premise processing with selected external integrations. It is important to make a conscious decision about which parts remain on-premise and where external services are or are not appropriate.

### What does ‘white-label hardware’ mean?

White-label hardware refers to existing or selected hardware that is not designed from scratch as the company’s own hardware product, but is chosen because its specifications are suited to the application. AITJE uses this as a basis to deliver a practical local AI solution.

The value lies not only in the device itself, but above all in the combination of hardware selection, software, configuration, AI functionality, access and management. ‘AITJE’ ensures that the solution is fit for purpose for the organisation and the process for which it is intended.

Developing hardware from scratch is often slow, expensive and unnecessary. For many AI applications, it is wiser to choose proven hardware and carefully design the software layer, configuration and AI workflow to suit it.

### How does this fit in with local AI?

Local AI requires hardware that is sufficiently powerful, stable and suitable for the task. By selecting the hardware based on its intended use, a solution can run locally without each application becoming entirely dependent on external platforms.

# What is RAG?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-rag

> RAG is a method whereby a language model first retrieves relevant information from documents or a knowledge base before providing an answer. As a result, answers are often more specific, better substantiated and more useful for your own organisation.

### What does RAG stand for?

RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. First, the system retrieves relevant information from a knowledge base, document collection or other source. Only then does the model use the context it has found to construct an answer.

### What happens from a technical perspective?

In a RAG system, a query is first translated into a search. Relevant text passages are then selected and sent to the model. The model therefore responds not only on the basis of its training, but also on the basis of sources retrieved at that moment.

### Why is this valuable?

A standard LLM does not automatically know what is contained in your manuals, policies or project documents. With RAG, the system can provide answers based on your own information. This makes AI much more useful for internal knowledge enquiries, document support and customer-focused processes.

### What determines quality?

The quality depends on the source data, document structure, search logic and whether the correct passages are selected. Poorly structured documents or out-of-date information will also result in substandard answers in a RAG setup. RAG is therefore not a panacea, but a process that must be properly organised.

### When is RAG not enough?

RAG helps with knowledge retrieval, but does not solve everything. For complex workflows, decision logic, rights management or actions in other systems, you often need additional layers, such as validation, human verification or agent logic. RAG is often a strong foundation, not the complete product.

[Contact AITJE](https://aitje.com/en/contact) — contact@aitje.com

# What is context in AI?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-context

> Context is all the additional information you provide to a model so that it better understands what you mean. Good context makes the difference between a generic answer and something that really suits your task, organisation or document.

### What constitutes context?

Context may consist of the question itself, previous messages, documents, instructions, examples, roles, company information or desired output. In practice, anything that helps the model provide a more targeted response forms part of the context.

### Why is context so important?

A model without context usually provides a general answer. As soon as you add your objective, source information and constraints, the same AI becomes much more specific. The quality of an answer therefore often depends less on the model alone and more on the context you provide.

### What types of context are there?

You might consider task context, such as exactly what the user wants; document context, such as relevant sources; and organisational context, such as tone of voice, policy or process agreements. The better these layers align, the more useful the output becomes.

### What often goes wrong?

Many applications provide too little, too much or the wrong context. Too little context results in superficial answers. Too much context makes the answer slow or muddled. The wrong context causes a model to go in the wrong direction, even if the question itself is logical.

### A practical rule of thumb

Provide only what is necessary to carry out the task properly. Think in terms of the decision or answer you wish to receive, rather than the urge to dump all the information at once. Good context is focused, relevant and up to date.

# What is a context window?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-context-window

> The context window is the maximum amount of information a model can process in a single interaction. This determines how much text, chat history or document fragments can be used at any one time.

### In plain language

You can think of a context window as a model’s working memory. The larger that working memory, the more text, previous messages and documents the model can take into account simultaneously to formulate a response.

### Why is this important?

With long documents, extensive chats and larger knowledge bases, you can quickly reach your limits. In such cases, not all relevant information can be included in one go. The system must therefore decide what to include and what to leave out.

### What happens when you hover over it?

If you try to provide more information than fits within the context window, the system will have to shorten, summarise or omit parts of the text. As a result, important nuances may be lost. In some cases, the model may then appear careless, whilst in fact it has simply been given too little useful context.

### Bigger isn’t always better

A larger context window is useful, but no guarantee of quality. If you add poor or irrelevant information, the answer will not automatically improve. Relevant selection, a good summary and clear instructions remain more important than simply having more tokens available.

### Practical implications

In real-world applications, the context window determines how you structure documents, how long a chat history remains usable and how you organise RAG or summaries. It is therefore not an abstract model detail, but a design choice with a direct impact on usability and reliability.

# What is an AI agent?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-ai-agent

> An AI agent is a system that not only provides answers, but can also take steps towards a goal. This includes retrieving information, making choices, using tools and carrying out a task partly automatically.

### More than just a chatbot

A chatbot usually responds to a question with text. An agent goes a step further and can carry out actions. These include searching for documents, creating summaries, retrieving data from a system, drafting responses or initiating a workflow.

### How does an agent usually work?

An agent often works using a combination of instructions, context, tools and decision-making logic. The system is given a goal, determines which step is logical, uses external functions or data where necessary, and then delivers a result or the next step.

### Where does the business value lie?

Agents are particularly useful for recurring tasks with fixed steps. They can relieve the workload on staff, reduce waiting times and make processes more consistent. The greatest value is realised when an agent is not a standalone solution, but is embedded within a clear process with defined permissions and limits.

### Where does the risk lie?

The more autonomy an agent is given, the greater the importance of logging, access management, validation and control points. An agent who is allowed to carry out actions in systems without clear guidelines can cause errors to escalate rather than resolve them.

### When it makes sense to start small

In many cases, it is wiser to start with a limited agent task, such as drafting proposals or preparing information. This allows you to learn where the system works well and where human oversight remains necessary. A good agent usually emerges from a clearly defined problem, not from a vague idea of complete autonomy.

# What are embeddings?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-zijn-embeddings

> Embeddings convert text into vectors so that systems can recognise pieces of information that are similar in content. They form an important foundation for semantic search and many RAG applications.

### In brief

Embeddings are mathematical representations of text. Rather than simply comparing words literally, a system can use embeddings to identify which pieces of content are similar in meaning. This makes it easier to identify meaning and relevance.

### Why are embeddings necessary?

Without embeddings, search often relies primarily on exact matches. This is limiting, as people can phrase the same question in many different ways. Embeddings help a system to recognise similarities in content, even when the words used differ.

### How are they used in RAG and search systems?

Documents are broken down into smaller sections, which are then converted into vectors. When a new question is asked, the system also creates a vector of the question and searches for text fragments that are thematically similar. This allows it to retrieve relevant context before the model provides an answer.

### What determines quality?

The quality depends on the embedding models used, how documents are segmented, how up-to-date the source data is and how the search layer is configured. Good embeddings do not compensate for a poor source structure. They work best when the entire knowledge chain is sound.

### What do you need to remember?

Embeddings do not provide answers in their own right. They primarily help to find the right information. Think of them as a technical foundation beneath knowledge bases, search functions and RAG systems, rather than as a standalone end solution.

# What is prompt engineering?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-prompt-engineering

> Prompt engineering is the deliberate formulation of instructions to ensure a model produces useful output. It is not about tricks, but about clarity regarding the objective, context, tone, preconditions and desired format.

### Why does the wording matter?

A model reacts strongly to how you describe a task. A vague question usually yields a vague answer. As soon as you specify your role, objective, tone, context and desired output, the result often becomes immediately more useful.

### What makes a good prompt?

Good prompts usually contain a clear task, relevant context, any constraints, examples and a desired output format. Not every prompt needs to be long, but it must be precise enough to provide direction.

### What is it not?

Prompt engineering is not a collection of magic phrases that always work. It is an iterative process of testing, refining and understanding how a model responds. In business applications, this often involves standardisation as well, so that teams can work more consistently.

### What is the business value?

Better prompts result in less rework, more consistent output and clearer use of AI within teams. This is particularly relevant when several staff members are working with the same system or when output needs to comply with internal standards.

### When do you scale this up?

As soon as an AI task becomes a recurring one, it is worth documenting, testing and refining prompts. Prompt engineering then transforms from a series of isolated experiments into a repeatable process that saves time and improves quality.

# What is an API?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-api

> An API is an agreed method by which systems exchange data or functions with one another. It is the interface that allows software to communicate with other software without the need for manual copying and pasting.

### In brief

API stands for Application Programming Interface. It is an interface that enables software to communicate with other software in a fixed, structured manner. This allows systems to securely retrieve or send information, or carry out actions.

### What does an API actually do?

Via an API, a website can retrieve customer data, call up an AI model, send documents or write information back to a CRM, ERP or other system. The user often does not notice this immediately, but behind the scenes it is a crucial connecting layer.

### API versus manual work

Without APIs, people often have to retype data, export it or carry out individual steps manually. With an API, systems can do that work automatically and more consistently. This saves time and reduces the risk of errors, provided the integration is set up correctly.

### What should you bear in mind?

Key points include permissions, authentication, error handling, logging, speed limits and documentation. An API may function technically but still be operationally impractical if management, security or monitoring are lacking.

### Why is this relevant to organisations?

Virtually every modern digital environment relies on APIs. If you understand what an API does, you can better assess how systems are linked, where dependencies lie and how flexibly a solution can be expanded in the future.

# What is a webhook?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-webhook

> A webhook is an automatic message sent from one system to another as soon as something happens. This allows you to trigger processes immediately without having to constantly check for new information.

### In plain language

A webhook is a notification that is sent automatically as soon as an event occurs, such as a new enquiry, payment, upload or form submission. Instead of constantly checking to see if anything has changed, you receive an immediate notification when it does.

### What is the difference between this and an API?

With an API, you usually actively request information. A webhook works the other way round: a system notifies you automatically that something has happened. In many integrations, you use both together: a webhook for the trigger and an API for the follow-up work.

### What do you usually include?

A webhook often contains information about the type of event, a timestamp, a record ID or a reference to additional data. Sometimes all the necessary information is contained within the webhook message, and sometimes another system needs to retrieve additional data via an API.

### What are the pitfalls?

A webhook must be delivered reliably and processed securely. You must therefore pay attention to verification, retries, logging and what happens if the receiving system is temporarily unavailable. Without these measures, a seemingly simple integration can still prove fragile.

### Why is this useful?

Webhooks make processes faster and more efficient. They are useful for notifications, triggering workflows, document processing and other situations where immediate follow-up is important. In well-designed systems, webhooks reduce delays and minimise unnecessary traffic.

# What is a backend?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-backend

> The backend is the part of the software where processing, logic, integrations and data flows run behind the scenes, out of the user’s view. It is the technical layer that ensures an app or website can actually do something.

### What do developers mean by this?

The backend is the layer behind a website, dashboard or app. This is where requests are processed, data is retrieved, business logic is executed and permissions are checked. The user does not usually see this layer directly, but it does determine how the system behaves.

### What is typically running in the backend?

Consider APIs, databases, authentication, logging, integrations with other systems, document processing and server logic. In AI applications, the backend can also handle prompt logic, context selection, RAG queries and the processing of model calls.

### Why is the backend important?

A good interface alone is not enough. If the backend is slow, insecure or poorly designed, the whole application will crash. The backend largely determines reliability, scalability and what is technically possible within a process.

### Which questions are relevant?

When considering quotations or choosing software, it is wise to ask where data is stored, how integrations work, how errors are handled and how logging or access rights are managed. These are typical backend questions that reveal a great deal about the maturity of a solution.

### How does the backend relate to the frontend?

The front-end is what users see. The back-end is what powers it. Together, they form the overall experience. A robust solution therefore not only has a polished interface, but also a back-end that is logical, secure and maintainable.

# What is a front-end?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-frontend

> The front end is the part of the software that users see and interact with directly. It encompasses screens, forms, feedback and interaction, and therefore relates to how user-friendly and intuitive a system is in practice.

### In brief

The front end is the interface of a website, portal, dashboard or app. It is the part that users interact with directly: buttons, forms, tables, navigation, notifications and other visual elements.

### Why is front-end development important?

Even if the technology behind it is robust, a solution can still be frustrating if the interface feels unclear or sluggish. Front-end development is therefore not just about appearance, but also about ease of use, clarity and trust.

### What will a user see as a result of this?

Users notice the front-end in terms of loading time, readability, error messages, the sequence of steps and how intuitive an action feels. A good front-end makes complex processes manageable. A poor front-end makes simple tasks unnecessarily difficult.

### How does the front-end work with the back-end?

The front-end collects input and displays results. The back-end processes that input and returns data or actions. Effective collaboration between the two ensures that a system not only looks good, but is also functionally sound and continues to operate reliably.

### How do you assess quality?

Look for clarity, speed, error handling, accessibility and whether the interface aligns with the actual work process. A good front-end isn’t impressive for its design, but makes sense in terms of usability.

# What is the cloud?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-cloud

> By ‘cloud’, organisations usually mean software, storage or computing power made available via external infrastructure. This offers flexibility, but also involves decisions regarding data, dependency and management.

### What exactly does that mean?

‘Cloud’ means that software or data does not run solely on your own device or server, but is provided via external infrastructure. This infrastructure is usually managed by a supplier or hosting provider and is accessible via the internet.

### Why do organisations choose this?

The cloud can be attractive due to rapid deployment, scalability and remote management. You do not need to host everything yourself and can often get started more quickly. This is practical for many applications, particularly when flexibility is more important than full local control.

### What factors need to be taken into account?

The cloud also raises questions about privacy, data location, recurring costs, vendor lock-in and availability. As soon as processes become truly dependent on external platforms, these choices become more strategic than they appear at first glance.

### Cloud or on-premises?

This is not usually a black-and-white choice. Some functions can run perfectly well in the cloud, whilst others must remain on-premises for reasons of continuity, security or cost control. In practice, a hybrid approach often emerges, with the most logical solution chosen on a process-by-process basis.

### What do you need to remember?

The cloud is not inherently good or bad. It is a way of organising infrastructure. The right choice depends on your data, your processes, your risk profile and how much control you wish to retain over the underlying technical layer.

# What is a workflow?

Official page: https://aitje.com/en/knowledge/wat-is-een-workflow

> A workflow is the fixed sequence of steps through which work, information and actions move through a process. Only once you have a clear understanding of your workflows can you truly assess where software, automation or AI adds value.

### In brief

A workflow describes how a task is carried out step by step. Think of data entry, checking, processing, approval, feedback and any follow-up. It is therefore not just about what happens, but also in what order and by whom.

### Why do you hear this so often with software?

Software often supports or automates existing workflows. If you do not understand how a process works, it is difficult to determine where a system should assist. That is why a workflow-based approach is important for bespoke software, integrations and AI applications.

### What makes a workflow effective?

A good workflow is clear, repeatable and takes exceptions into account. Roles, inputs, decision points and checkpoints are then visible. This makes a process less dependent on individual knowledge held by staff members.

### Where does AI come into the picture?

AI is particularly useful in parts of a workflow where language, classification, summarisation or preparation play a role. There is little point in haphazardly adding AI without understanding where the real bottlenecks and quality risks lie.

### Common mistake

Organisations sometimes look at the tools first and only then at the process. That can easily lead to automating the wrong things. It is better to get the workflow right first and then determine which steps can best be supported by software, integrations or AI.
